#9081. Please Don’t Sit on the Flowers

Long-lost Georgia O’Keeffe landscape goes to auction, Brancusi gets lost at MoMA, interview with Doris Salcedo, and is showing at documenta worth it?

Sitting at September Cafe, I watch the autumn leaves separate from the trees and get carried away gently by the wind. They swirl and twirl, performing a merry little dance in the air before falling to their final resting place.

News has just come in about a sweeping Democratic victory in the midterm elections, as fierce and awesome as a Gustave Courbet wave. But I see nobody popping champagne bottles in the streets. A pregnant black cat with a hanging belly saunters by.

Lying back in the dentist’s chair, a TV screen in front of me shuffles picturesque views from exotic places. They're idyllic to the point of not looking real. My doctor, a Lebanese, shows me an X-ray of my mouth, which looks like Beirut at the height of the Civil War.

The sky over the Robert F. Kennedy Bridge is gray, and the Harlem River is brooding as I make my way to Taryn Simon’s exhibition Father Country I Do Love You at the Guggenheim Museum. The show tells the heroic tales of an FBI agent whose alleged career intersects with major events in American history. Cold, antiseptic photographs encased neatly in plexiglass make up a detective story linking the protagonist to the explosion of TWA Flight 800, the 9/11 attacks, the bombing of the United States embassy in Nairobi, Bill Clinton’s impeachment, and more. Trudging up the Guggenheim’s spiraling galleries, I wonder whether this patriotic show is organized and sponsored by the US State Department. Simon makes you read a lot, but all that reading is just meant to distract you from thinking.

Jodie Foster narrates the audio guide for those who don’t have the patience to read long-winded wall texts. At the cafeteria, while eating a bikini sandwich, I see a woman who looks exactly like Judi Dench, another actress. “I love storytelling,” she tells a friend before plunging her teeth into a chocolate croissant.

On my way out, I once again resent how this museum forces everyone to exit through the gift shop to encourage commerce, but I buy myself a $5 Guggenheim bag anyway. Outside, in one of the manicured gardens of the Upper East Side, a small sign pleads, “Please don’t sit on the flowers.”

I cross the street into Central Park through Engineers’ Gate, climb the steps past a gilded bust of John Purroy Mitchel, NYC mayor between 1914-1918, and look out over the Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis Reservoir. I think of the Kennedys, of Trump, and of Simon. A worker collects brown leaves in plastic bags and tosses them into a truck wrapped in a photo of green leaves. A mother tries to snap a photo of her child, but the unruly kid refuses to pose for the camera. He throws a fit, falls, and, to her shock, ends up sitting on the flowers.

Over the past few months, several artist friends who have been invited to participate in the upcoming documenta 16 have contacted us for advice, asking whether they should accept, refuse early on, or accept for now and withdraw at a later stage. As two artists who participated in documenta 15, we understand the dilemma. An invitation to documenta is not something one receives thoughtlessly. It is hard to turn down, and these days, it is also becoming hard to accept. | Anonymous Documenta 15 Artists

#9080. French court orders restitution of Pissarro painting sold at Sotheby’s for £1.2m to heirs of Jewish banker

Camille Pissarro's Darse de pêche et bassin Duquesne (fishing dock and Duquesne basin, 1902)

A French court has ordered the cancellation of the Sotheby’s London sale of a landscape by Camille Pissarro, and its immediate restitution to the heirs of Jewish banker Salomon Flavian, on the grounds that it was looted in Paris in 1941. According to the 5 November ruling, Sotheby’s has two months to reveal the “complete identity” of the buyer, subject to a daily penalty of €1,000 for any delay.

Entitled Darse de pêche et bassin Duquesne (fishing dock and Duquesne basin, 1902), this view of the port of Dieppe in Normandy, was sold at Sotheby’s London on 25 June 2024 for £1.2m.

The Sotheby’s catalogue did mention it had been owned by Flavian from 1935 and was registered in the Répertoire des biens spoliés (repertory of looted art) released by the French government in 1947. Nevertheless, it indicated that the work was “offered for sale pursuant to a settlement between the current owner and heirs of Salomon Flavian”. Their consent, Sotheby’s explained in court, had been obtained by the Mondex Corporation, a Toronto-based company specialised in the return of looted art.

At a court hearing on 18 September, Corinne Hershkovitch, the lawyer for seven heirs of Flavian, said this agreement had been signed by only two relatives and the others were not consulted. In court, Mondex and Sotheby’s endorsed a study which concluded that the painting had been acquired in the late 1930s by the British artist and collector Edward Le Bas, from the dealer Paul Rosenberg, and therefore was no longer part of Flavian’s collection seized in 1941 by the Nazis.

The court judged otherwise, considering that there was “no direct and convincing evidence” of these alleged transactions. On the contrary, the Flavian family’s research produced “a set of precise, serious and concurring elements demonstrating that Pissarro’s work was indeed looted during” the Second World War, according to the judges.

In a statement, a spokesperson for Sotheby’s London said it is “disappointed by the judgement regarding the restitution”. However, the auction house “welcomes the decision to dismiss all claims against Sotheby’s”. “The history of the artwork is complex”, the spokesperson adds, and “we fully recognise the profound losses suffered by the Flavian family during the Nazi era and, from the outset, have approached this matter responsibly and with the care and respect it deserves.”

“It is a very important ruling, which opens the way to a restitution that the Flavian family has demanded since the war,” Hershkovitch tells The Art Newspaper. “It shows Mondex’s failure in its mission, and now Sotheby’s has to bear the responsibility for having sold a looted artwork.”

Mondex’s lawyer, Melina Wolman, says the company intends to appeal a judgement that, she says, is “posing major difficulties in regard with historical factors”. She adds that the name of Le Bas, who owned the Pissarro painting in the 1950s, appears on an entry in the catalogue raisonné edited by Paul Rosenberg in 1939. But the court ruled that this was only one among “contradictory elements” and that Sotheby’s and Mondex “did not support this hypothesis by any direct proof of such sales, at a time when France was at peace and the art market well structured”.

In court, Remi Sermier, a lawyer for Sotheby’s, also disputed the court’s jurisdiction on a sale made in London. But the court stated that, under French law, the annulment of the 1941 dispossession acts makes all subsequent sales of the work null and void. However, the court chose not to cancel the agreement signed between Mondex and the two heirs who had waived all their rights to the painting just before the sale, in exchange for a share of the sale price.

The ruling could trigger a cascade of ligitation internationally. Sotheby’s is “considering whether to join the appeal”, a spokesperson says, stressing that “client confidentiality is of paramount importance” for the company and it is not ready to willingly disclose the identity of the painting’s buyer. The spokesperson adds: “There is a procedure that will need to be followed in order to enforce the decision in the UK.”

In case of success, the Flavian family will have to face the current possessor, who can demand compensation from Sotheby’s. For its part, the auction house could turn against Mondex and the consignor of the work, because, according to sources close to the case, the settlement agreement Mondex and the seller signed contains an indemnity clause of which Sotheby’s is the beneficiary.

Most estate planning advice assumes you will work until 60-65, accumulate wealth gradually, and have employer-provided benefits until Medicare kicks in. The FIRE path breaks every one of those assumptions. You may stop working at 35, 40, or 50 — meaning your estate plan must cover a potentially 40 to 50-year retirement, not the 20 to 25-year retirement conventional planning addresses.

This extended timeline creates unique vulnerabilities:

The SECURE Act fundamentally changed how inherited retirement accounts work, and this change matters enormously for FIRE households that have built large tax-advantaged portfolios.

Before the SECURE Act, non-spouse beneficiaries could "stretch" inherited IRA distributions over their own lifetime, allowing decades of tax-deferred growth. Now, most non-spouse beneficiaries must withdraw the entire inherited IRA balance within 10 years of the original owner's death. For a beneficiary in their peak earning years, this compressed timeline can push them into the 32% or 37% tax bracket on every distribution.

The FIRE advantage: Early retirees have years — sometimes decades — of lower taxable income between leaving work and taking Social Security or required minimum distributions. This creates a golden window for Roth conversions that no conventional retiree has.

A married couple who retires at 40 with $1.5 million in a traditional 401(k) and a $500,000 Roth IRA could systematically convert $80,000 to $100,000 per year from the traditional to the Roth, staying within the 22% bracket. Over 15 years, they convert $1.2 million to $1.5 million at a known, relatively low tax rate. Their heirs then inherit a Roth IRA that is completely tax-free — even under the SECURE Act's 10-year distribution rule.

Without conversions, those heirs would owe ordinary income tax on every dollar withdrawn from the inherited traditional IRA, potentially at 32% or higher if they are working professionals during their peak earning years. The tax savings for heirs can easily exceed $200,000 to $400,000 on a $1.5 million inherited traditional IRA.

Key Roth inheritance rule: Inherited Roth IRAs are still subject to the 10-year distribution rule, but the distributions are tax-free. The 10-year clock starts the year after the original owner's death.

A revocable living trust is the foundational estate planning tool for FIRE households. It provides three critical benefits that matter more for early retirees than conventional retirees:

Every early retiree needs three healthcare documents executed before leaving their employer:

Once you cross the $1 million net worth threshold — common in the FIRE community — asset protection becomes essential. You have decades of retirement ahead during which a lawsuit, car accident judgment, or liability claim could threaten the wealth you worked so hard to build.

For FIRE households pursuing charitable giving, a donor-advised fund (DAF) allows you to front-load charitable deductions in high-income years (or Roth conversion years), reduce your taxable estate, and distribute grants to charities over time. A DAF contribution is irrevocable and immediately reduces your estate while giving you advisory control over future grants.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Do not wait until traditional retirement age to complete your estate plan. The moment you leave employer benefits, you need a fully executed will or trust, healthcare directives, powers of attorney, updated beneficiary designations, and umbrella insurance. Many FIRE retirees leave their jobs with $1 million or more in assets and no estate plan in place. Every day without these documents is a day your family is exposed to probate, court-appointed guardianship, and preventable tax consequences.

Absolutely. If you have any assets, dependents, or strong preferences about medical care, you need at least a will, healthcare directive, and power of attorney. If you have reached FI with $500,000 or more in assets, a revocable living trust adds significant value through probate avoidance and incapacity protection.

Most non-spouse beneficiaries must now withdraw the entire inherited IRA or 401(k) within 10 years of the original owner's death. This compressed timeline can push heirs into high tax brackets. Roth conversions during your lifetime eliminate this tax burden because inherited Roth IRA distributions are tax-free.

For most early retirees, transferring your primary residence to a revocable living trust makes sense. It avoids probate on the home, enables seamless management if you become incapacitated, and does not affect your mortgage, property tax, or homestead exemption in most states. Consult your estate attorney about your state's specific rules.

Umbrella insurance provides liability coverage above the limits of your auto and homeowners policies. A $1 million umbrella policy typically costs $200 to $300 per year and protects against lawsuits, car accident judgments, and liability claims that exceed your underlying policy limits. For FIRE households with significant assets, it is one of the most cost-effective forms of protection available.

Yes, and early retirement is often the best time to do them. With no employment income, your taxable income is low, allowing you to convert traditional IRA or 401(k) balances to Roth at the 10%, 12%, or 22% bracket. This is significantly cheaper than the 32% or 37% rate your heirs might pay on inherited traditional IRA distributions.

Review your estate plan every three years at minimum and immediately after any major life event: marriage, divorce, birth of a child, death of a beneficiary, significant change in net worth, or a move to a new state. Early retirees have a longer planning horizon, making regular updates even more important than for conventional retirees.

Estate planning for early retirees is not a modified version of conventional retirement planning — it is a fundamentally different discipline. You face a longer incapacity window, a bigger healthcare gap, more exposure to tax law changes, and decades of asset protection needs. The FIRE community excels at building wealth through savings rate optimization and investment discipline. Apply that same rigor to your estate plan: execute foundational documents before leaving your job, optimize beneficiary designations for the SECURE Act, pursue Roth conversions during low-income years, and protect your assets with umbrella insurance and trust structures. The wealth you built deserves a plan that survives as long as your retirement.

#9078. An Interview with Surreal Salon 18 Winner, River Reishi

We are so excited to share our interview with Surreal Salon 18 winner, River Reishi, selected by guest juror, Swoon. On the occasion of the win, we spoke with Reishi about the work in the show, the history of Surreal Salon, and her upcoming travels.

Juxtapoz: Congrats on the big win! Talk about the winning work, what the story behind it is, the process, and even the process of submitting it to the Surreal Salon?River Reishi: The piece is called Surface Tension. It shows a figure emerging from dark water, her hands reaching forward as if she is about to break through the surface and step into our world. She is half submerged, suspended in that strange moment between two realms. Around her is an ephemeral field of black sand and amber.

From land, the surface of water looks smooth and transparent, almost empty. But of course it hides an entire world that is not ours. I have always been fascinated by that threshold. The installation tries to hold that exact moment where the two worlds meet.

The sculpture also glows faintly from within, which was a little hard to see in the bright gallery lighting but becomes visible as you approach. I like that quiet surprise. The piece looks still at first, but there is a sense that something is about to happen. Water is often a symbol of life, but it also carries danger and power. Louisiana and the Gulf region know that reality very well. I think some of that tension found its way into the work.

The black sand surrounding the sculpture is loose and hand-drawn into patterns, so the installation only exists in that form for a short time. Even small vibrations change it. I am interested in that fragility, in works that cannot quite stay fixed.

It was already an honor to be included in a show curated by Caledonia Curry (Swoon). When I arrived to install the piece and saw the other works for the first time, I remember thinking how haunting and memorable every single one was. So hearing the piece announced as Best in Show later that night felt surreal in the truest sense.

Had you followed the Surreal Salon in past years? What did you know about it? I had heard about the Surreal Salon through the pop surrealist art community for years, but this was the first time I lived close enough to attend in person. I kept hearing that it felt a little like an unofficial kickoff to Mardi Gras season, that people came in elaborate costumes and that the whole evening had this celebratory, slightly otherworldly atmosphere.

What I did not realize until participating this year was that some people actually design their costumes based on the artwork in the exhibition. That was amazing to see. At one point someone came up to me wearing a costume inspired by my piece, and getting to watch him model it and explain how the sculpture influenced the design completely made my night. It felt like the work had briefly stepped out of the gallery and into the room!

Also, it was a wonderful addition to have SWOON be the juror for this year's contest. I have done it in the past, and it was hard, fulfilling work. What did you know of SWOON's work and did that inform your submission at all? I have admired Swoon’s work for a long time, especially her installations and the way she moves between sculpture, architecture, and public intervention. I first heard about her in 2009 when she brought the Swimming Cities of Serenissima project to the Venice Biennale. A fleet of sculptural rafts floating into one of the most formalized spaces in the art world was such an unforgettable gesture.

The act of arriving that way, without waiting for institutional permission, became part of the artwork itself. That kind of boldness has always stayed with me. It is difficult to break into the art world, especially in spaces where voice is carefully selected and curated. Seeing an artist carve out space for herself so creatively was incredibly inspiring.

I also love the direction her work has been taking recently with the Sibylant Sisters project. My own work is deeply inspired by myth and storytelling, so it has been fascinating to watch her develop that world, creating her own oracle cards and building a living mythology around the work. There is something powerful about artists inventing symbolic languages that people can enter into. So having the chance to meet her and have her encounter one of my installations was a very meaningful moment for me.

You work in a few different mediums, and sculpture and installation seem to be your focus. Talk a little bit about your process and where you feel most comfortable as a maker? I am not sure I feel comfortable in any single medium, and I think that is probably a good thing. I tend to move toward whatever material feels necessary for the idea at hand. In many ways my practice grew out of practical constraints. For a long time I did not have a large studio, so I had to find ways of making work that could expand into a space temporarily and then disappear again. Sand, modular sculptural elements, and ephemeral materials all emerged from that reality.

Over time those limitations became part of the language of the work itself. I am drawn to materials that hold a sense of fragility and transformation. Installation allows me to build an environment around the sculpture where those ideas can unfold more fully, where the viewer is not just looking at an object but stepping into a moment or a story.

What sort of artists influenced you as you began to find your own voice? And, sort of as a nice anecdote, what is the last work that made you stop in your tracks and get back into the studio and create?

Voice is an interesting concept to me as a woman, because women often face particular obstacles when it comes to the emergence of voice. It takes a certain measure of audacity to say something and commit it to art. In a way you are asking the world to listen. Because of that, I am especially inspired by women who make art without asking permission.

I mentioned earlier how powerful it was for me to learn about Swoon bringing her Swimming Cities project to the Venice Biennale. That gesture has always stayed with me, not only because of the work itself but because of the confidence behind it. The willingness to claim space in a world that does not always easily offer it. Moments like that remind me that voice is not only about what you say as an artist, but about allowing yourself to say it at all. That idea continues to shape the way I approach my own work.

As for the last artwork that made me stop in my tracks, I recently visited the Museo Nacional de Antropología in Mexico City. Walking through the galleries of figurative ceramics from different regions of Mexico was completely mesmerizing. The Mayan ceramics in particular took my breath away. There is so much spirit in them, such a sense of presence. I encountered one ceramic face that affected me deeply. I have gone back to see it several times now, and each time I leave feeling more inspired to return to sculpture.

What else do you have lined up this year? Are you someone who likes to work in a gallery situation, or do you prefer alternative means to show your work? This summer I will be working with Raf Gallery in Reykjavik, Iceland during the month of August. A total solar eclipse will pass directly over Reykjavik on August 12, and later that month the city celebrates Menningarnótt, a large citywide festival of arts and culture.

Raf Gallery works with both artwork and Baltic amber jewelry, and I have always been drawn to amber as both a material and a mythological object. For the exhibition I will be installing sculpture and a sand installation that tells the myth of the birth of Baltic amber while also reflecting on eclipse mythology and the relationship between darkness and light.

The sand will come from the local shoreline, and at the end of the exhibition I invite the community to dismantle the installation with me. We carry the sand back to the ocean and return it with a wish, prayer, or intention.

I love Iceland deeply. The black sand I often use in my installations was inspired by the volcanic beach at Reynisfjara, so being able to create work there during such a rare celestial moment feels very meaningful.

As for where I like to show my work, I enjoy many different contexts. My installations have appeared in galleries, museums, empty storefronts, and even city halls. But my favorite place for ephemeral work is the beach.

When I lived near the sea in Washington State, friends and I would sometimes build temporary altars from flowers, driftwood, shells, and plants as offerings to the water. The tide would slowly carry everything away. There is something very special about building something together that only exists for that one night.

What did you like about the whole Surreal Salon experience? What were some of the highlights?The whole evening had an incredible energy. The costumes alone were extraordinary, and everywhere you looked there was another small moment of creativity unfolding. Music, conversation, artists reconnecting, people discovering work for the first time. It felt celebratory in the best way.

There was also an unexpected moment early in the night. Someone accidentally backed into the platform holding my installation, and when the platform shifted the sand vibrated and many of the detailed designs disappeared. Thankfully the person who tripped was completely fine, which was the most important thing. But in a strange way the moment also revealed something essential about the work. Some people had assumed the sand had been glued down or painted in place. When it shifted, it suddenly became clear that the entire surface was loose and hand-drawn. I sat beside the piece and carefully repaired it, re-drawing the patterns into the sand and amber while people watched.

For me that moment captured the spirit of the work. The installation only existed in that exact form on that particular night. It could be recreated, but it would never be exactly the same again. Everyone there was witnessing something temporary, something that belonged only to that moment in time. And in a way that felt very fitting for the Surreal Salon itself.River Reishi is a multidisciplinary artist whose sculptures and ephemeral sand installations explore myth, grief, and the mysterious threshold between worlds. Drawing on feminine water deities and ancient storytelling traditions, she works with materials such as sand, amber, and light to create environments that exist only briefly in time.See more at riverreishi.com and on Instagram @riverreishi.

#9077. Lacaton & Vassal wins Le Prix Charlotte Perriand 2027

The Créateurs Design Association & Awards has named Pritzker Prize-winning French studio Lacaton & Vassal Architectes the recipient of the Le Prix Charlotte Perriand 2027.

Lacaton & Vassal Architectes, which is led by architects Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal and known for its social housing designs, was recognised for contributing to contemporary architecture by transforming and improving existing buildings.

The Créateurs Design Associates (CDA) said the studio’s work improves “living conditions while preserving resources and architectural heritage”.

The duo said it was “very happy” to receive the award.

“Charlotte Perriand’s tireless pursuit of comfort, well-being, and the pleasure of the inhabitant and of everyday life, her modernity, and her political commitment to exposing poor housing conditions and to transmission and education remain profoundly relevant today and are a source of inspiration,” Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal said.

“Her manifest spirit of openness and freedom touches us deeply. We are very happy to receive this distinction.”

The architects founded their studio in 1989 and have since worked on high-profile projects such as the transformation of the Palais de Tokyo in Paris, the Nantes School of Architecture and the Cité du Grand Parc housing transformation in Bordeaux.

The latter, which was completed with Frédéric Druot and Christophe Hutin, won the European Union’s Mies van der Rohe Award in 2019.

Lacaton & Vassal Architectes’ other social housing projects include the renovation of the 1960s Tour Bois-le-Prêtre tower block in Paris, also in collaboration with Frédéric Druot, which was completed in 2011.

It also converted and extended a former shipbuilding workshop to create the FRAC Nord-Pas de Calais contemporary art gallery in Dunkirk.

The Le Prix Charlotte Perriand was established in collaboration with the family of the late architect and recognises practitioners whose contributions have advanced architecture and design.

“In awarding Le Prix Charlotte Perriand to Lacaton & Vassal, the CDA members recognise the care and imagination with which they approach the places people call home. Their work shows how much can be gained by understanding what is already there,” Créateurs Design Association co-founder Meredith Xavier said.

The award will be given to Lacaton & Vassal Architectes in a ceremony on 16 January 2027, at the Shangri-La Paris. Architect Kengo Kuma will also be honoured at the event as the winner of the Andrée Putman Lifetime Achievement Award 2027.

Lacaton & Vassal Architectes has previously won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2021, as well as the 2023 Soane Medal for architecture.

Last year, Lacaton won the 2025 Jane Drew Prize for women in architecture.

#9076. Kohei Yamada: MY SCREEN TESTS @ Gr Gallery, New York (UPDATED with Installation Imagery)

GR gallery is pleased to present My Screen Tests, the first New York City solo exhibition by Kohei Yamada. The exhibition examines the enduring value of the authentic relationship between artist and artwork, engaging in themes of irony, introspection, and visual metaphor, which draw inspiration from contemporary practice and Yamada’s nuanced admiration for American Pop art.

Presenting a new suite of paintings on canvas -each paired with its esquisse on paper- In My Screen Tests, Yamada searches within New York City’s identity as the art capital of the world in order to infuse his work with a distinct vitality, revealing his admiration for Andy Warhol through motifs referencing the Silver Factory era and its entourage, and evoking tension between a sense of historical prestige and vibrant pop expressions. This interplay initiates a critical conversation between perceptions of art and is worthwhile in examining the creative directions of today’s world.

My Screen Tests is defined by motivations that comment on the ambiguous nature of art’s true value beyond its creator, while also alluding to Yamada’s need to remain bound to art for the rest of his life. The work also critiques the world’s normalization of deceit and capitalistic greed, alongside a persistent

longing for freedom that remains just out of reach. New York City lies at the core of Yamada’s practice, serving as both subject and catalyst for exploring the interplay between personal perception and nostalgia. It also functions as a cultural bridge between American and Japanese influences, tracing the artist’s journey from childhood through his engagement with the legacy of Andy Warhol, as well as other Japanese and American artists. Through a combination of brushwork, abstraction, and figuration, Yamada weaves a narrative rich in contemporary art history, while also confronting the true value of an artist’s existence.

Over half of the works exclusively made for My Screen Tests are imbued with references inspired by Warhol’s practice and artistic values, cast against New York City as a hub for experimentation where art meets and even challenges commerce. Repetition and humor are also at the core of the artist’s creative process, adding a wittiness and discipline to his work, while also connecting it on a deeper level to the Pop tradition. Yamada draws upon the city as both muse and stage, invoking a range of artistic influences as main characters, while ultimately revealing each to be a projection of his own identity.

The opening reception will take place on Friday, May 15 from 6:00 pm to 8:00 pm. The artist will participate in the opening reception.

#9075. Eight architecture and design events in November from Dezeen Events Guide

Miami art week, Design Doha Biennial, Dubai Design Week and the Dezeen Awards 2026 party are among the key architecture, design and art events featured in Dezeen Events Guide this November.

Other events taking place during the month include Collectible New York, Cairo Design Week, Irish Design Week and BDNY.

Dubai Design Week celebrates its 12th edition in 2026, returning with a programme of fairs, exhibitions, installations, talks and markets.

The festival’s headline event Downtown Design takes place from 4 to 8 November in the city’s design district and welcomes brands such as Trika Arabia, Bottega Living, Biscuit, Alain Ellouz Paris and 1971 – Design Space.

Other events in the lineup include the competition-winning Urban Commissions installation by Dubai-based NAO Architects and the In Other Words group exhibition.

5 November 2026 to 31 Janaury 2027, Qatar

The second edition of the Design Doha Biennial celebrates design, architecture and craft from the Middle East, North Africa, and South Asia (MENASA) region.

The festival programme features exhibitions, talks, installations, awards and other pop-up events, including the latest edition of Arab Design Now, which showcases projects from 81 participants.

#9074. Whitney Museum selects a staff curator and a stage director to lead 2028 biennial

Meg Onli and Zack Winokur Photo by Bryan Derballa

The Whitney Museum of American Art has selected Meg Onli, a curator at the museum, and Zack Winokur, a choreographer and director for the stage, to curate the 2028 edition of the Whitney Biennial. It is due to open in March 2028.

“Every Whitney Biennial springs from a distinct curatorial alchemy,” Scott Rothkopf, the Whitney’s director, said in a statement. “Meg is one of the most compelling curatorial voices working today, with an extraordinary ability to champion artists and bring fresh perspectives to the history of American art. Zack is an equally inventive artistic programmer who has become one of the leading voices of his generation through groundbreaking work across opera, theater, dance and the visual arts. Their partnership promises a radical new vision for the 2028 Biennial.”

Onli is one of the Whitney’s star curators, having joined the institution as a curator-at-large in 2023, then as a curator in 2024. She co-curated the 2024 Whitney Biennial, titled Even Better Than the Real Thing, with fellow Whitney curator Chrissie Iles. Most recently she co-curated the museum’s current Roy Lichtenstein retrospective (until 10 May 2027).

“From the Whitney’s early Annuals to its many subsequent iterations, the Biennial has a rich history of reinvention that is already giving us much to think about,” Onli said in a statement. “I couldn’t be more excited to explore what the Biennial can be alongside Zack, who is such a dynamic thinker, and to see where our conversations with artists lead.”

Winokur’s work spans dance, music, visual art, opera and theatre. He is the co-founder and artistic director of the performing arts collective AMOC* (American Modern Opera Company), which last year staged a five-week takeover of the Lincoln Center campus on Manhattan’s Upper West Side. He was previously the artistic director of Little Island, a park and cultural event space designed by Heatherwick Studio and MNLA that rises out of the Hudson River not far from the Whitney. His projects for the stage and screen have included directing productions at Opera Philadelphia and the Santa Fe Opera, and working on the expanded version of The Wizard of Oz currently showing at Sphere in Las Vegas.

“I’m honoured to be curating the Whitney Biennial with Meg,” Winokur said in a statement. “Our shared desire to centre objects and people and the collision between them already echoes our collaboration. It’s that energy that makes the dialogue with her so fun and inspiring. As an artist, what excites me most is being in service to other artists, and I’m delighted to have the opportunity to do so in the context of the Whitney.”

The 2026 Whitney Biennial, which was organised by staff curators Marcela Guerrero and Drew Sawyer, closed in October. It was seen by more than 550,000 visitors, according to the museum’s figures, around 75% of whom identified as either Millennials or Gen Z, making it the youngest audience since the Whitney started tracking visitors’ ages.

The exhibition’s 2026 edition was also remarkably controversy-free, though the exhibition is often a lightning rod for debates, protests and political statements. The 2019 edition was led by Whitney curators Jane Panetta and Rujeko Hockley, and came to be known colloquially as the “tear gas biennial” due to weekly protests and participating artists’ threatened withdrawals over the Whitney’s vice chairman at the time, Warren Kanders, who was the chief executive of Safariland, a defense and security contractor that manufactured tear gas canisters that had been deployed against asylum-seekers at the Mexico-US border, among other materials. Kanders eventually resigned from the museum’s board; he is currently the chairman and chief executive of Cadre Holdings, a Florida-based manufacturer of security and law-enforcement equipment.

The 2017 Whitney Biennial, which was co-curated by Christopher Y. Lew and Mia Locks, was largely overshadowed by the wide-ranging debate over a single painting in the exhibition: Dana Schutz’s Open Casket (2016), in which the artist portrayed the famous image from 1955 of 14-year-old Emmett Till lying in an open casket following his brutal abduction, mutilation and murder. The artist Hannah Black wrote an open letter criticising the work’s inclusion in the biennial and calling for its destruction, sparking protests inside and outside the museum and arguments about censorship, identity and cultural appropriation.

The 2028 Whitney Biennial will be the 83rd edition of the exhibition, which started out as a series of medium-specific exhibitions before becoming the Whitney Annual in 1937, then transitioning to its every-other-year format in 1973. It remains the most closely watched recurring exhibition of contemporary art in the Americas.

The Whitney Museum has turned to two in-house curators to put together a show that celebrates diversity in American art—but as in 2017, the biennial is already mired in controversy

The 82nd edition of the most closely-watched recurring exhibition in the United States will open in spring 2026

After a 2022 Biennial curated entirely in-house, the Whitney has selected one staff member, Iles, and an independent curator, Onli, to organise the exhibition’s 81st edition

#9073. Solid cork forms walls of pavilion dedicated to silence at Casa No Tempo in Alentejo

Photography by Mercês Tomaz Gomes

Antwerp-based studio Corkinho has unveiled its latest “still room”, a pavilion with walls of solid cork, which is installed in the grounds of a vacation villa designed by Manuel Aires Mateus.

The still room is a space dedicated to silent and introspective activities, such as reading, yoga, tea ceremonies or meditation.

Corkinho installed it in the grounds of Casa No Tempo, a former farmhouse in southern Portugal, which architect Aires Mateus converted into a holiday home in 2014 for hospitality entrepreneur João Rodrigues.

Lead designer Cédric Etienne devised the building’s innovative structure, which is fully demountable, with the help of architect and master carpenter Gonçalo Madeira Marrote of Madeiguincho.

The floor slab is a timber deck, built over a foundation of removable concrete blocks.

Above this, solid blocks of cork are stacked up like giant bricks to form the building’s walls and secured with metal rods that thread through milled channels.

The pavilion is topped by a timber roof, described by Etienne as “like a hat with four screws”, which helps to weigh down the cork blocks.

“I wanted it to be zero waste and carbon-neutral,” the designer told Dezeen.

“If we need to dismantle it, we can place it somewhere else. There is no glue and no screws,” he said.

“It’s like the Japanese way of building teahouses, with total respect of the local materials and no harm to the land.”

As the name suggests, Corkinho is a studio that specialises in objects and spaces built from cork.

The studio first launched the still room concept in 2020, when it moved its office into the former Noorderpershuis power station in Antwerp and transformed one of the rooms into a silent sanctuary.

Etienne defines a still room as any space where you can pause your mind and be still.

“It’s a place where you disconnect from noise and distractions and invite a deeper sense of presence,” he said.

After consulting with various hotel brands keen to adopt the concept, Etienne pitched the idea to Rodrigues and his company, Silent Living.

The company has five properties, all designed by Aires Mateus and all with a focus on slow living.

“I had been to Casa No Tempo many times, so I knew the place like an inner home,” the designer said.

“It felt so aligned in terms of feeling and senses, so I thought it could be a really beautiful challenge to move the concept forward in this place,” he continued.

The room can be used by guests staying at the villa, but it can also accommodate curated programmes.

Etienne has been hosting four-day silent retreats, allowing groups of designers and hospitality professionals to learn more about the still room concept.

The cork blocks, supplied by locally based company Sofalca, were heat-treated to improve their durability. The material gives the building impressive sensorial and thermal qualities, Etienne said.

“All the technical properties of cork – the acoustics, the scent, the softness – all become architectural conditions,” he stated.

“You really feel like you’re coming into a womb. Even when it’s 40 degrees outside, the temperature inside is around 22 or 23.”

Other pavilions recently featured in Dezeen include a wildlife pavilion informed by rippling water and a jigsaw-like pavilion made of mass-timber scrap.

Photography by Mercês Tomaz Gomes

#9072. Many London architecture firms not paying London Living Wage

The majority of the London-based studios in The Pay 100‘s fifth annual salary survey are not paying Part I architectural assistants the London Living Wage, as required by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA).

An engineering firm has topped the leaderboard for the average salaries for UK architects, according to a survey conducted by the anonymous group The Pay 100.

Engineering firm tops architect salary leaderboard

Published over the weekend, the survey provides rough figures only based on the mean figures submitted by respondents. This year’s data collected the annual salary of 127 firms in the UK and the mean number of hours of unpaid overtime per week.

Topping the leaderboard with the highest average annual salary for architects with less than five years’ experience is BakerHicks, an engineering and design firm, which paid £72,000, according to the survey.

Second on the list is London studio Hawkins\Brown at £63,700, and joint third at £56,300 are London practices Samuel Chisholm Studio and Thomas Alexander Design.

The survey also presented figures for Part I and Part II architectural assistants. Transport for London had the highest wage for Part II roles at £44,000, followed by Foster + Partners at £42,000.

Majority of London firms not paying London Living Wage

The results for Part I roles included salaries from 30 studios, 21 of which were based in Greater London.

Only the top four studios on the leaderboard – Haworth Tompkins, Allford Hall Monaghan Morris, Studio McW and Studio PDP – paid more than the London Living Wage of £32,136, which RIBA declared a requirement for relevant offices.

Twelve of the 30 studios were paying Part I roles less than the £29,328 UK Living Wage.

Low wages “a threat to the future of the profession”

Alongside its survey data, The Pay 100 wrote an open letter to RIBA, asking it to take action on the financial wellbeing of those working in the architecture industry and to ensure the long-term future of the profession.

“Our aim has always been to create tangible financial incentives for employers to improve pay, empower employees to make informed career decisions, and encourage a healthier, more sustainable profession,” said The Pay 100 in the letter.

“We recognise that architecture practices operate within a highly competitive market, often under significant financial pressure themselves,” it continued. “Nevertheless, the commercial challenges facing practices should not prevent the profession from addressing the deteriorating conditions experienced by many employees.”

“Poor financial conditions for staff are not merely an employment issue; they are a threat to the long-term health, resilience and future of the profession.”

It went on to set out two courses of action it called for RIBA to take: establishing “meaningful minimum salaries” for RIBA chartered practices, and taking full ownership of The Pay 100 and its annual salary survey.

The Pay 100 said a framework of minimum salary levels should be established across different architecture roles, increasing year-on-year in line with inflation.

“A profession cannot sustainably advocate for the value of its services while leaving the financial conditions of its workforce to market pressures alone,” it said. “The RIBA should take a leading role in addressing this imbalance.”

After five years of aiming to improve pay transparency with its annual surveys, The Pay 100 wants RIBA to take ownership of the survey and commit resources to it, developing it into an industry-wide initiative.

“We believe that improving pay transparency across UK architecture should be a core responsibility of the profession’s leading membership body,” said The Pay 100.

“Under the RIBA’s stewardship, the survey could benefit from significantly greater reach, sustained institutional support and broader participation across the profession,” it continued.

“This would provide a foundation for more comprehensive salary data, stronger engagement between employers and employees, and meaningful progress towards better financial conditions throughout the industry.”

The Pay 100 ended its letter by asking for a public response from RIBA by 1 December

As part of Dezeen’s Performance Review series, we investigated how architecture fees became so low and the impact this has on professionals.

#9071. Art Collector Barbara Jakobson’s Famous Upper East Side Townhouse On the Market for $9 Million

Barbara Jakobson was a monumental force in the New York art world for over 60 years, serving as an influential collector, a fierce patron, and a longtime trustee of New York’s Museum of Modern Art (MoMA). She also had a sharp, curatorial eye and a truly singular style. That is perhaps best evident in her home on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, which doubled as her own ever-evolving gallery from the mid-1960s until her death in 2025.“I see the house as a vessel for an ongoing autobiographical exercise,” Jakobson told Curbed in a 2021 interview. “I keep the transformation as proof of life.” Related Articles R.M. Schindler's Modernist Beach House, Built for a California Health Nut, Hits the Market for a Breezy $18.8 Million Art Collector and Publisher Benedikt Taschen Lists Mid-Century Modern Beverly Hills Home for $25 M.

The five-story townhouse along East 74th Street in the Lenox Hill neighborhood was built in 1910 and later expanded by architect John Kingsland in 1956. Prior to Jakobson, filmmaker Elia Kazan lived in the 20-foot-wide abode while directing East of Eden (1955) and Splendor in the Grass (1961). Hollywood stars including James Dean, Natalie Wood, and Marlon Brando reportedly visited then.

Jakobson, a native New Yorker, bought the pad in 1965 and lived there for nearly six decades. During that time, she welcomed New York’s creative set, such as artists Jasper Johns, Andy Warhol, Cy Twombly, and Robert Rauschenberg. After her death last summer, the property was brought to market in April 2026 for $9.8 million. It received a price cut of over $800,000 before reaching its current asking price of $8.99 million. Leslie Hirsch, Edward Joseph, Howard Morrel, and Benjamin Anderson of Christie’s International Real Estate New York hold the listing.Nicknamed “the Squirrel House” on account of the bronze squirrel sculptures at the entrance, the home is whimsical yet refined. Red lacquered doors open to 6,000 square feet of stylish interiors, with eight bedrooms and six full bathrooms spread throughout.A grand entry hall with triple arches and custom wallpaper by artist Peter Halley leads to a parlor floor featuring a formal living room, a gallery, and a salon with a wood-burning fireplace. A staircase—on which Jakobson was photographed for Vogue—spirals down to a spectacular double-height great room, where an outline of Frank Stella’s 1971 Felsztyn III remains. It once hung there but was sold in 2005 at a Christie’s auction featuring works from Jakobson’s collection. Glass doors lead out to a private 350-square-foot garden.The guest bedrooms, including two junior suites with dressing rooms and en suites, sprawl across the next two levels. The primary suite, meanwhile, covers the entire top floor, offering a light-filled private lounge for reading, relaxing, or even pondering art.

#9070. Brick bathhouse by Kengo Kuma nears completion in Copenhagen

Pyramidal towers frame pools at the Kai Water Culture House by Japanese studio Kengo Kuma & Associates, which is nearing completion in Copenhagen.

Set to open on the city’s harbour in December, the 5,800-square-metre aquatic centre will contain ten indoor and outdoor pools, alongside wellness facilities and cultural spaces.

Kengo Kuma & Associates was commissioned alongside Danish firms Cornelius Vöge, Søren Jensen and Vilhelm Lauritzen Architects to realise the new cultural and recreational facility on the city’s artificial island of Christiansholm – known locally as Papirøen, or Paper Island.

Photos revealed ahead of the opening show the facility’s five staggered buildings perched atop a glazed base and fronted by a wooden pier that provides direct access to the sea.

“The Water Culture House is a significant new landmark on Copenhagen’s waterfront,” Kengo Kuma & Associates lead architect Yuki Ikeguchi said. “It is part of the story of the city and the harbour’s transformation from an industrial to a cultural harbour.”

“As the cultural cornerstone of Papirøen, the house is a gathering place with water and community as its focal point, embraced by a public harbour bath,” Ikeguchi added.

Constructed from 300,000 handmade bricks, the tapered volumes are punctuated by triangular and square openings that filter dappled light into the indoor pools.

“The bricks are arranged in a staggered, stepped pattern, giving the building its distinctive texture and sculptural character,” Vilhelm Lauritzen Architects said.

“A total of 403 windows of varying sizes act as viewing apertures, framing the surroundings and creating captivating experiences of natural light as it shifts throughout the day,” it added.

The tallest of the five volumes, dubbed the Culture Tower, houses the centre’s cultural programmes, which include a third-floor events space. Meanwhile, the other four towers each house lofty indoor pools.

Nestled between the five brick volumes on the first floor is an outdoor pool, framed by the building’s sloped facades, and an open-air Onsen – a Japanese-style hot spring – that overlooks the harbour.

The Kai Water Culture House is set to open to the public on 5 December, with its wooden pier slated for completion early next year.

The facility sits among a wider redevelopment of Copenhagen’s Paper Island led by Danish studio COBE. Recent projects on the island include a 20,000-square-metre apartment complex informed by the area’s 300-year-old warehouses.

Alessandro Carloni and Erica Rivinoja on reinventing a book everyone thinks they know, and the one problem that could have sunk the whole film.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Turning a Dr Seuss illustration into a fully realised 3D world is harder than it sounds, and directors Alessandro Carloni and Erica Rivinoja knew what they wanted to avoid on Warner Bros. Pictures Animation’s new The Cat in the Hat movie: CG that simply imitates a picture book.

“We didn’t want to use CG to just ‘simulate’ an illustration,” Carloni says of making the new 2026 animated movie. The aim was for audiences to feel the familiarity of Seuss’s painterly illustrations while experiencing the depth and immersion of modern 3D animation.

The creative partnership behind the film was just as collaborative. Asked how they divided the writing and directing duties, Rivinoja says they didn't split the work between them. “It was less ‘divide and conquer’, and more ‘unite and conquer’. To streamline the process, we were usually in meetings together.”

Working with Autodesk software such as Maya and Flow was key, as revealed in a new video series called Made to Make, which has now been expanded to include more behind-the-scenes details; watch it on the Made to Make YouTube channel.

Put simply-ish, it meant rethinking lighting, surfaces and even the edges of objects. The team paired simple, almost flat surfaces and key lighting with softer, more volumetric fill and bounce lighting. They also developed a stylised, painterly edge treatment to avoid the harsh sharpness of digital imagery. Then came realistic lens behaviour, including halation, aberration, and lens flare, which Carloni says helped ground the images in believability. The team developed the combination specifically for the film, creating its own visual style.

Maya sat at the pipeline's centre. Production designer Aidan Sugano’s hand-drawn designs were translated into 3D models there, and everything in the film, from characters and props to entire worlds, was built in the software.

For the animators, Maya was also the only way to touch the characters. Marek Kochout, for example, shaped the Cat’s performance through the Graph Editor, where a single expressive shot can involve hundreds of layered curves. The Pose Library let animators save and reuse expressions and attitudes, and over time it became a shared reference for how the Cat moves, with standout scenes added so every animator could draw on them.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Keeping a film like this on track across four countries, with teams in India, Montreal, London and Los Angeles, fell to Autodesk Flow Production Tracking, which followed every character, environment, prop and version from boards through to final compositing over roughly two years. Sugano, in New York, and VFX supervisor Matt Waters, in London, used RV within Flow Production Tracking to review the same footage in real time. Executives and partners screened the film through PIX, now part of Autodesk Flow Capture, whose watermarking and access controls helped keep it under wraps. As Carloni puts it, “This movie would not exist without the tools we had.”

For a fuller look at the workflow, visit Autodesk’s blog on the making of the film.

For Rivinoja, preserving Seuss's visual language was essential. The team wanted fans to recognise his signature design motifs, from hatch marks and negative space to his colour palettes, arches and mechanical hands. “We wanted to make sure people who love the books saw something of the book in the film,” she says.

It wasn't going to be a straightforward page-to-screen adaptation, though. The filmmakers wanted to expand the world and make it a cinematic spectacle, exploring what happens after the original story ends, including where the Cat goes when he leaves the house. They came up with the idea that entertaining bored children is his job, which explains why he shows up at the house on a rainy day. He's also one of many specialists at the company, and his famous hat is actually his company uniform.

The film also needed several distinct environments: the real world, Seuss’s world and three further worlds connected to characters in the story. Rather than altering the characters to suit each setting, the team kept their designs and shape language consistent.

“We kept consistent shape language throughout, and we didn’t change the looks of the characters,” says Rivinoja.

The differences come from colour, surfacing, rendering style and lighting, Carloni explains. The characters stay recognisable while the emotional feel of each world changes as the story progresses.

Carloni says the hardest problem was making sure audiences would want to spend time with the Cat, explaining: “To make sure the character of the Cat was truly lovable. The kind of character anyone would want to spend time with. If we loved him, we had a movie. If he's unlikable, then no matter how fun the story or how fantastic the adventure, the movie would never work.”

He describes animation's greatest advantage as the same thing that makes it daunting: ultimate freedom. “There are limitless possibilities. You can literally do anything at all in animation. As the saying goes, the only limit is your imagination, which makes it perfect to tell a Seuss story and create a Seuss world.”

The Cat in the Hat arrives in cinemas and IMAX in North America on 6 November 2026, with international releases beginning on 4 November.

#9068. Jaguar designs Knightsbridge flagship to be "physical expression" of Type 01 electric car

Photography courtesy of Jaguar Land Rover

British car brand Jaguar has redesigned its flagship store in Knightsbridge, London, which is the only place in the world where the public can see the recently unveiled Type 01 electric car.

Jaguar overhauled itp show in central London to align its aesthetic with its latest electric car, which was created as the first car in a new era for the brand. It aimed for the flagship store to be a clear departure from the traditional car showroom.

“[We wanted] to create a physical expression of the new Jaguar,” said Jaguar Land Rover spatial brand design team senior manager Nick Rolls, whose team was responsible for overhauling the store.

“Rather than a traditional showroom, we wanted to design a destination where architecture, culture, hospitality and craftsmanship come together – and London felt like a natural home for that vision,” he continued.

“The space has been purpose-designed from the ground up to embody the brand’s new identity – it gave us the opportunity to truly rethink what a Jaguar destination could be outside traditional conventions.”

The showroom has space for two cars to be displayed, one of which is currently the Type 01, with the showroom being the only place in the world where it is on display to the public.

However, the majority of the ground floor of the space is occupied by a restaurant.

Named Café Eighty-One, the restaurant by Michelin-starred chef Michael O’Hare was finished in rich red fabric.

Upholstered benches run around the space, while a series of booths line the front facade of the showroom.

“Food is one of the most universal forms of connection,” said Rolls. “We wanted Café Eighty-One to be a welcoming space where people could spend time, meet friends or discover something new.

“It’s designed to be a destination in its own right, helping make Jaguar at Knightsbridge part of London’s cultural and hospitality landscape,” he continued.

According to Rolls, the extensive use of red was a nod to the surrounding brick architecture in central London.

“Jaguar’s design philosophy is exuberant modernism, so colour plays an important role in creating emotion, atmosphere and a sense of occasion,” he said.

“The rich reds within Café Eighty-One were inspired by London’s iconic red-brick architecture, which is so prevalent throughout Knightsbridge and the surrounding neighbourhoods,” he continued. “It was a way of connecting the interior to its setting while creating a warm, vibrant environment that feels distinctly London.”

Through the rest of the spaces, the materials and colours were chosen to directly evoke the interiors of the Type 01 electric car.

“The relationship is deliberate,” said Rolls. “The interiors share the same emphasis on materiality, craftsmanship and bold, contemporary form that defines Type 01.”

“Materials such as travertine, tactile textiles and warm brass reference the vehicle’s interior, while the use of sculptural shapes, carefully composed lighting and strong geometric forms reflects the same creative philosophy behind the car,” he continued.

While the public restaurant and showroom space are on the ground floor, a lower level contains more private spaces for sales, meetings and for discussions about customisation.

One of these, called the Design Vault, was entirely finished in rich navy blues.

Overall, Rolls hopes that the revamped space will help people understand the current, major rethink that the brand is embarking on.

“I hope people leave with a deeper understanding of Jaguar,” he concluded.

“Every element of the destination has been designed to reflect craftsmanship, creativity and bold design. We want people to feel a genuine connection to the brand and to see Jaguar through a new lens.”

The creation of the showroom follows the launch of Jaguar’s second electric car earlier this year, the Type 01. The car is the production version of the much-discussed Type 00 concept car, which drew much attention in 2024 when it was unveiled following a rebrand for the car company, which was described as a “complete reset”.

#9067. Federal Judge Temporarily Blocks Construction of Trump’s Arch, Hours After it Gains Final Approval

A federal judge has temporarily blocked construction of President Donald Trump’s triumphal arch just hours after a hastily convened planning commission granted the project final approval.

U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a restraining order Friday morning halting construction of the 250-foot arch for 14 days, giving the court time to consider lawsuits challenging the project’s legality. The order bans all activities related to the project, including excavation, utility installation, and road closures around its proposed located, Memorial Circle near Arlington Cemetery. The administration has been given a Monday, November 9, deadline to guarantee its compliance with the ruling. Related Articles Trump Convenes Final Review for Triumphal Arch, Seeks Immediate Start on Construction Arlington County Board Files Lawsuit to Stop Construction of Trump's Triumphal Arch

The National Capital Planning Commission, composed mostly of Trump loyalists, approved the project on Thursday after a nine-hour virtual hearing in which more than 100 people testified, including military veterans, D.C. preservationists, and family members of those buried at Arlington. The outcome was widely expected, prompting opponents to seek federal court intervention before the review process had concluded. Their appeal succeeded: Judge Chutkan will consider several independent legal challenges to the arch, including one brought by the governments of D.C. and Virginia and another by Vietnam War veterans.

The lawsuits argue that the Trump administration bypassed the necessary congressional approval and failed to adequately assess the project’s potential impacts on the surrounding landscape. Critics have raised concerns about air and noise pollution, traffic disruptions, and other problems stemming from the structure’s height and location. They argue that the arch would interfere with flightpaths from DCA and, particularly controversially, disrupt the carefully cultivated visual relationship between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

According to an October investigation by the Washington Post, which used a to-scale 3D model to map the arch’s shadows, the structure would cast shadows across more than 75,000 graves at Arlington over the course of the year, as well as several major memorials, including those dedicated to John F. Kennedy and Martin Luther King Jr., and the Vietnam Veterans and Korean War Veterans memorials.

The Trump administration has argued that the arch would serve as a necessary commemoration of the nation’s 250th anniversary of independence and enhance security in Washington, D.C. In recent weeks, Trump proposed that the structure could double as a “military complex” equipped for snipers and drones. The final plan submitted to the commission, however, reportedly omitted those details.

Mark Paoletta, a White House official and the commission’s chairman, called the empty space at Memorial Circle a “national disgrace” on Thursday and praised the president’s “historic vision.”

Construction is projected to take two to three years, with crews working nearly around the clock, according to the Trump administration.

#9065. Anxiety Tattoos: How Ink Therapy Can Help Ease Mental Health Struggles

Tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry. For some peeps, they’re the go-to for commemorating life wins or solidifying deep-seated beliefs — from quotes that got you through dark times or portraits of your fave pets.

The act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience. The machine’s buzz and the needle’s sharp sting are part of a ritual that may help bring internal battles to the surface. But is there a link between anxiety and the decision to get tatted? Could framing your fears and anxieties in gorgeous designs help you cope? Continue reading to find out.

For many, tattoos are much more than art. Peeps who have anxiety may get tattoos as a way of taking control over their narrative, including their mental health struggles.

Anxiety disorder makes life challenging, and you may feel you’re stuck in a rip tide of continual worry, fear, and dread. Even if you know it’s the anxiety talking, you can still struggle to contain these overwhelming feelings, and it’s exhausting. Anxiety can trick your mind, tell you you’re unworthy, and there’s no way out.

But here’s where tattoos come into play — they create a visual shoutout to your strength and resilience. Imagine marking your skin with reminders of the battles you’ve won and what you’ve overcome.

Getting inked can feel like grabbing the reins back from anxiety and stress. A tattoo is an affirmation. It can turn your invisible battle scars into something tangible and beautiful, giving a sense of ownership over your body and experiences. This is huge when anxiety tries to convince you that you don’t have a say in your own story.

Whether it’s a poignant quote, a symbolic image, or just a badass design, a tattoo packs a punch of personal significance and your enduring strength. You’ve taken a deliberate, proactive step to help you take greater control over your life, and that should be celebrated.

Psychologically, tattoos are visual high-fives to yourself. For the anxious folks, tats are a way to take those messy, abstract feelings and pin them down in something real and tangible.

There’s also some evidence to suggest that the pain involved in tattooing can be cathartic, offering a physical release for emotional pain. This could explain why people who self-harm or live with substance misuse or eating disorders might be drawn to the tattoo chair — it’s a place where psychological pain is acknowledged and artistically transformed.

Research suggests there may be correlations between tattoos and mental health.

One 2013 study involving 65 female participants living with anorexia, bulimia, and binge eating disorder explored the relationship between eating disorders, self-injury, and tattoos. Around 51% of the participants reported a history of self-injury, and 27% had at least one tattoo. Those with tattoos were more likely to have a history of self-harm, so the authors suggested that tats could be a form of self-punishment.

However, in an interesting twist, 27% of those with tattoos showed no history of self-injury. These peeps reported more positive body image, higher self-esteem, and fewer mental health struggles.

The relationship between tats and mental health is complex and still being decoded. Further research would help confirm the link between the two.

Tattoos can swing either way on the mental health seesaw. For some folks, getting tattooed is symbolic of their healing process. It says, “Hey, I’ve been through some stuff, but look how I’ve grown!” These tattoos often become symbols of a deeply personal journey, spotlighting moments of triumph over anxiety and depression.

But here’s the flip side: if someone gets inked on a whim or during a rough patch without much thought, that tattoo could be a permanent reminder of a not-so-great time.

In a 2011 study of 82 peeps getting their first tattoo, researchers measured their feelings about their appearance and body both before they got the tattoo and then again immediately and three weeks after the tattooing. The findings showed that right after getting their tattoos, folks of all genders experienced a decrease in appearance anxiety and dissatisfaction. Three weeks later, they reported increased body appreciation, a stronger sense of having a distinctive appearance, heightened feelings of uniqueness, and improved self-esteem. However, female folks experienced increased anxiety related to how others viewed their physique 3 weeks post-tattoo, while males reported a decrease in this type of anxiety.

These results suggest that getting a tattoo can positively affect mental health, but of course, the impact varies among individuals.

Tattoos can be an artistic strategy to enhance your mental health game, but it’s crucial to take a beat and really think it through before you get inked.

Whether you’re looking to mark a milestone, manage the mayhem of anxiety, or remind yourself that everything will be okay, a carefully considered tattoo can be a meaningful addition to your narrative, helping you manage anxiety and positively shaping your story.

#9064. Arches create “animated silhouette” at red-brick apartment block in King’s Cross

Two-storey-tall arches frame entrances to Cadence, a mixed-use apartment block in King’s Cross, London, which has been completed by local studio Alison Brooks Architects.

Positioned at the northern end of Lewis Cubitt Park, the prominent red-brick building combines 163 apartments alongside commercial and social spaces organised around an open-air courtyard.

Signposted by its two towers, the building by Alison Brooks Architects forms part of the wider King’s Cross redevelopment and is complete with views overlooking Heatherwick Studios’ Coal Drops Yard to the south.

According to studio founder Alison Brooks, the building’s red-brick exterior was chosen to pay homage to the nearby St Pancras Station, while its arched openings draw on the area’s neo-gothic architecture and were conceived as a “civic welcoming gesture”.

“The main concept of the project was to make a clear statement of welcome and arrival in King’s Cross, but from the north end of the master plan rather than the south end, which everybody is familiar with,” Brooks told Dezeen.

“My first instinct was to respond to King’s Cross’ iconic railway station architecture, sculpting the site massing to create an animated silhouette. A language of two-story high arches creates a really generous, welcoming gesture at street level and toward the park,” she added.

The building is formed of a five-sided block, with no designated front or back, which rises to form two towers reaching 12 and 16 storeys respectively.

For its construction, the studio opted for a Design for Manufacture and Assembly approach, which saw 85 per cent of the building’s components prefabricated off-site.

At the centre of its angular plan, an open-air courtyard, complete with a reflecting pool, has been wrapped by sheltered walkways that provide a shared circulation space between the building’s private and commercial programmes.

“It’s a multifaceted building,” Brooks said. “Each facet of the pentagon has a particular identity or address to the space that it’s adjacent to.”

“This idea of making a very connected space at the base of the building, even though it’s a courtyard, is visually trying to connect all the sides of the plot to the city around it.”

“It’s a place of movement and light and also a kind of special quality because of the reflecting pool,” she added.

The building’s first two floors have been dedicated to 633 square metres of commercial and social spaces, which include a “community living room” that opens onto the courtyard at ground level.

A prefabricated lift system connects to the upper floors, where the 163 residential units benefit from both courtyard and street views.

A combination of rectangular and arched windows draws daylight into the building’s white-walled interior, complemented by private balconies and communal roof terraces.

Other projects developed as part of the King’s Cross regeneration include Google’s landscraper office building by architecture studios BIG and Heatherwick and an office block designed by Coffey Architects to recall the area’s industrial spaces.

#9063. Rome’s Galleria Borghese’s $11.15 M. Extension Is Moving Forward Despite Pushback

Rome’s Galleria Borghese is getting too popular for its own good. The 17th-century villa museum has launched an architectural competition for an extension, reports Le Figaro.

The decision is a result of an influx of tourists. Each year, the museum has 700,000 visitors, 60 percent of which are international. The museum houses paintings, sculptures, and antiquities from works by Bernini and Caravaggio to Canova and Raphael.

“Until now, we have had to cap daily attendance at 2,000 people, allowing entry only to those who have booked online,” Francesca Cappelletti, the museum’s director, told the French newspaper. “Yet, every day, we see groups of international visitors in the park who are disappointed to find they cannot enter because there are no spots left.” Related Articles A Late Baroque Master's Lost Marble Turns Up in a UK Salvage Yard Italian Prime Minister's Face Erased from Rome Fresco After Vatican Complains

The new extension is being created with support from Rome’s Ministry of Cultural Heritage and the municipality. It estimated to cost $11.15 million (€10 million). The space will span 3,000 square meters and will help the museum exhibit work that’s sitting in storage, as well as stage exhibitions, open a restaurant or bookstore, and a laboratory. “We cannot alter the existing heritage; the solution must involve a contemporary structure. After all, look at the Louvre pyramid in France—it works perfectly,” said Cappelletti in regard to the extension. The structure is meant to blend in with the villa’s distinct white style and surrounding park.

The competition for the extension is being organized by the Italian engineering firm Proger Spa, also a patron of the museum. The deadline for candidates to express their interest in the competition is November 13. “Naturally, it is not the company, but rather a jury of independent experts and renowned international figures that will select the winner in mid-May 2027. We have no intention of relinquishing our role; the final decision rests with us. That said, every effort must be made to ensure that Italian public funds remain protected,” said Cappelletti.

But not everyone is a fan of the plan. “It is a grotesque proposal. It is blasphemy,” Alix van Buren, president of the Friends of the Villa Borghese association, told the Times of London. “The villa is one of the most perfect, unalterable artistic ecosystems that human genius has ever created. Not a single pin can be moved without upsetting the balance.”

Michele Campisi, the general secretary of the Italia Nostra heritage group, joined in on the fury, calling the plans “bizarre” and arguing that the museum is trying to compete for popularity with the Colosseum. Tomaso Montanari, an art history professor at the Universita per Stranieri di Siena, described the extension as “moronic” in the Italian newspaper Il Fatto Quotidiano, adding that it was like “building an extension on Brunelleschi’s dome” at Florence Cathedral.

Fabio Rampelli, the vice-president of Italy’s lower house of parliament and a key ally of Prime Minister, Giorgia Meloni, called for Cappelletti to resign in a Facebook post. “Treating a space like this as if it were your own back garden is dismal,” he said.

We've spotted lots of Google Easter eggs over the years. Hidden animations, fun widgets and even playable games have surprised us in the search results for particular queries. Sometimes they're quickly discovered when they're designed around trending search topics, but some less obvious gems can pass under the radar, continuing to surprise unsuspecting users.

We just discovered a gem on a topic that's close to our own hearts. Here at Creative Bloq, we consider ourselves something of an authority on design fails. We've written about enough of them over the years, from disastrous rebrands to AI adverts.

So imagine our delight when we discovered that typing the term 'design fails' into Google delivers results presented in one of the world's most controversial typefaces.

I say one of the most controversial fonts, because these days we would much rather have Comic Sans back in place of that generic AI font that's cropping up on flyers everywhere.

Putting Google's joke aside, the typeface has its place, and not every use of Comic Sans is a design fail. Indeed, many designers have come out in defence of Comic Sans over the years.

It was created in 1994 by Microsoft in-house designer Vincent Connare to solve a specific design problem. He needed a suitable font for the dog in the Microsoft Bob interface – Times New Roman just didn't suit the pup's playfulness, so Vincent created a comic book-inspired font to match the cartoony design.

Mimicking informal, handwritten speech in cartoons, it was perfect for injecting levity into casual communication pieces for schools, community spaces, standing out from stuffy serifs and dull sans serifs while also being very clear and readable thanks to its wide spacing.
