#9043. A New Hudson Valley Art Space Promises to Be As Accessible as It Is In Flux

Less than two blocks from the Katonah train station stands a nondescript, gray two-story building on one of the main drags of this Hudson Valley town. Emblazoned in a kerned-out serif font, its name, Branchline, belies what awaits inside: a public-facing exhibition space for the Gochman Family Collection (GFC).

Established just five years ago, the GFC has already become one of the world’s leading collections of contemporary Indigenous art, with more than 850 works. Until now, works from the GFC have primarily hung in the New York apartment of Becky Gochman, the collection’s founder and custodian, and her family, though some 200 works are typically on loan to institutions around the world at any given time. The GFC has generously opened the home to museum groups, schools, and artists for tours and events as a way to bring more attention to Native artists, but the organization’s ambition has always been to make its holdings as accessible as possible. Related Articles Leah Ke Yi Zheng Joins Antenna Space, Pérez Art Museum Miami to Honor Nicolas Berggruen, and More: Industry Moves for October 28, 2026 Elisa Nuyten's Vega Foundation Is Quietly Reshaping the World of Moving-Image Art

“It’s one thing to articulate a mission, but what matters to me,” GFC creative director and curator Rachel Martin (Tlingít) said Thursday during a press preview, “is if I’m putting that language out into the world [then] I’m making sure that our organization is following that with action.” She added that she sees Branchline as a place for “bringing community together, which means making the Native community feel like they are very much a part of what the decision-making parts of this are, and then also inviting the community of Katonah to come in and learn about new artists that they might not have heard of.”

Anticipating that many visitors will arrive via Metro-North, the GFC named the space after the rail term “branch line,” or the place “where paths diverge and new paths begin,” as GFC director Laura Phipps put it. “We were excited about all the sort of ideas that ‘branch line’ conjures—both thinking about the metaphor of the train and the metaphor of trees—and what we can do to experiment and grow in this space.”

Free to the public, Branchline is taking its time to grow into its new digs, which will eventually total 10,000 square feet across four buildings. Friday evening’s inauguration will show off the first completed space, as well as plans for expansion in the coming months across an L-shaped plot that runs from the main building’s entrance on the Parkway to Katonah Avenue. The building houses a three-room gallery on the ground floor, two bedrooms upstairs for invited artists to determine how they want to spend the time, and a nearly operational ceramics studio downstairs.

Architectural renderings on view Thursday afternoon show that the building’s back door will open onto a small sculpture deck leading to a yet-to-be-built barn, where large-scale works will go on view. (The original barn was in such bad shape that it had to be torn down to make way for an exhibition space.) The barn will in turn lead to the Annex, which will take a more experimental approach (more on that later). From there, visitors will turn left onto a patio and eventually reach the back entrance of Twig, a retail store and café.

For now, visitors will get a taste of Branchline’s ambitions through a more traditional offering. Inaugurating the modest, nearly 2,000-square-foot gallery is “Line Break,” curated by GFC assistant curator Moonoka Begay (Ndee + Diné) with collection associate Nicole van Brugge. “Lines are a core facet of all visual language,” the exhibition’s introductory wall text begins, but Begay and van Brugge look past the formal qualities that a line and its breaks contribute to a work. Instead, they treat the line as a metaphor for lineage and bloodlines, borders and cartographic marks, horizons and sound barriers.

A tight show of 28 works by 18 Indigenous artists, “Line Break” offers visually compelling juxtapositions of artists from different generations working in a range of mediums and styles. Jaune Quick-to-See Smith’s The Spaniard (1988), a semi-abstract aerial view of the Flathead Indian Reservation in Montana, hangs next to Sara Flores’s Untitled (Shao Pei Maya Kené), 2024, a painting rendered in the geometric abstract visual language of the Shipibo-Conibo people, whose designs, according to an exhibition brochure, “map the community’s local worldview, environmental understanding, and cosmology.” Farther along are Teresa Baker’s Echoes (2024) and George Morrison’s Night Shadows. Red Rock Variation: Lake Superior Landscape (1994). Both are brightly colored abstract meditations on landscape made in very different mediums: acrylic, yarn, willow, and artificial sinew on AstroTurf for Baker; acrylic on canvas on board for Morrison.

Even the most seemingly formal works reveal their secrets as you delve deeper into how these artists use lines to make meaning. Across from the Quick-to-See Smith and Flores works are two pieces from Nadia Myre’s “Code of Construction” series, in which the artist arranges strung ceramic cylinders into squares depicting the ground-to-air distress signals for “Require Map and Compass” and “Not Understood.” Myre’s choice of medium draws on the tradition of wampum belts, used by Indigenous communities of the Northeast Woodlands to communicate political relationships. Myre’s work finds an analog in Faye HeavyShield’s the red line II (2025), a strand of red beads that the artist strung by hand. Here it is displayed in a coil, though its configuration is flexible—perhaps a metaphor countering the seeming immutability of shape, form, and even time.

The exhibition reaches its crescendo at its center with Raven Chacon’s Storm Pattern (2021–24), a handwoven wool textile accompanied by a multichannel sound piece whose low hum visitors have been hearing since entering the gallery. In 2016, Chacon noticed the sounds made by drones flying over the Oceti Sakowin camp at Standing Rock, where protesters had gathered to oppose the Dakota Access Pipeline. Ranging from loud and piercing to soft and soothing, the sounds of police surveillance drones mingled and merged with those of the protesters’ countersurveillance drones. In that harmonious dissonance, Chacon saw a score, which he recorded and also translated into the woven textile, charting the drones’ erratic flight patterns in a traditional Diné weaving style and structure.

Rounding out “Line Break” are two elements that will likely look drastically different in a few months. The GFC commissioned Matthew Kirk to make a site-specific work for an exterior wall of the building along an alleyway. Across three plywood panels, Kirk has collaged painted tar paper in various abstract forms and shapes. The work was already showing its ephemeral quality on Thursday morning, the paper having warped in the light rain.

A few steps down the alleyway is the Annex, which is still under construction: the plywood is exposed, and power cords run to jerry-rigged lightbulbs that illuminate its two floors. Rather than hide this rawness, the GFC team has decided to embrace it. For now, the Annex is home to a small show of drawings by Shuvinai Ashoona, who maps imagined scenes—ones that could perhaps one day come true—onto the Arctic landscape where she lives in Nunavut, Canada. The team acknowledged that it hasn’t quite figured out how the space will look in the near term, even once the build-out is complete. That will depend on how artists interpret a prompt that gives them the autonomy to do what they want.

“What GFC is doing is not trying to become an institution,” Martin said. “It’s trying to just meet where things are needed, and a space is definitely needed for art that is outside of the white box that you’re used to seeing, so that’s what we’re offering.”

#9042. How Going Blind Made Doris Salcedo’s Art Bigger and Better

Doris Salcedo is best known for her moving “anti-monuments,” gigantic artworks—or sometimes negative spaces—that propose new ways to commemorate atrocities. Always, she focuses on the victims’ perspectives. Her best-known work, Shibboleth (2007), installed in Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall, comprised one giant, scar-like crack in the concrete, rerouting foot traffic in a manner that evoked the jarring disruption of borders more broadly.

The Colombian artist began working at such a monumental scale only after she began losing her central vision. At age 31, Salcedo was diagnosed with Stargardt disease, a rare genetic condition, and today she is legally blind, with only peripheral sight. Related Articles Sophie Calle, Doris Salcedo Among Winners of $105,000 Praemium Imperiale Award Doris Salcedo Deserves Better Than Her Current Fondation Beyeler Survey

In November, at White Cube Gallery in New York, Salcedo will premiere a sculpture that is the culmination of decades of this collaborative way of working—and huge in a way that could never be accomplished by one person. A full-sized house—at nearly 30 feet—has been woven entirely from human hair. When I visited, dozens of assistants were working across her three studios, tying knots in individual strands, a painstaking process. The resulting pattern resembles chicken wire or a chain-link fence.

Even working with such a big team, the process took three years. “To be thankful is not enough,” Salcedo said of the collective effort, adding that it could have easily taken 20 years to make on her own—and that she couldn’t spare that kind of time at her age.

As Salcedo led me through her studio—her own iconic salt-and-pepper curls rhyming with the looping locks lining the space—she told me that all of her workspaces were designed by the architect Carlos Granada. The two have been working together for 25 years. He is also the architect behind Fragmentos, Salcedo’s 2018 “anti-monument” commissioned by her national government to commemorate the 2016 Colombian peace agreement. Visiting the building in the heart of Bogotá, what at first looks like a typical modernist, single-floor gallery takes on new weight in the feel of its flooring: The textured tiling is made from firearms that once belonged to the Colombian guerrilla group FARC and were later melted down. Visitors walk right on top of these instruments of violence and fear, on tiles Salcedo made in close collaboration with 20 Colombian women who survived sexual violence during the conflict.

The work has an undeniably chilling effect. School groups flock to it regularly. Some critics, though, have found its message misleading, since several splinter factions are still active and thousands of fighters rejected that 2016 agreement. But for Salcedo, Fragmentos is not a static space: She regularly invites other artists whose work resonates to exhibit within its walls. When I visited, a crew was de-installing a sound installation by Hajrah Waheed that filled the space with movingly hummed songs of resistance. The work, titled Hum II (2023), is surprisingly affecting, unifying: You’re made to feel something of the song’s sentiments even if they’re in languages you don’t understand. Fittingly, the title means “we” in Urdu, Waheed’s mother tongue.

Like Fragmentos, Salcedo’s studios boast high ceilings. Her workspaces also feature glass brick walls and floating staircases: These are sparse spaces that enable her and her team to see what they are working on. As she walked me through, magnifying glass in hand, she pointed out that one of her studios is the same shape as the home she is building—a triangle atop a square, as if a kid drew a house. Eventually, we came upon the net-like hair arranged in sections like a gradient, growing darker and denser at the bottom. She let me touch it, and I was surprised to find it so sturdy and lightweight at the same time.

THE WORK-IN-PROGRESS MARRIED a complicated process to a simple shape. As we spoke, I found myself wondering about the latter—why a house? I found a hint in two books sitting on the surface of her desk, both of them scanned so she can see them on a screen in large print: Domicide: The Global Destruction of Home and Dreamhouse: Stories of Art and Shelter.

House is not her first work on the subject of the devastating effects of the global housing crisis. Uprooted (2020–22), her prize-winning work in the 15th Sharjah Biennial (where, as it happens, she met Waheed, a fellow prize winner), repurposed 804 dead trees into a mesmerizing, if uninhabitable, home. At almost 1,000 feet long, the work is meant to speak to the predicament of climate refugees. Her newer work, which takes the same shape, is about more deliberate displacement: specifically, “domicide,” which the authors of one of the books on her desk, J. Douglas Porteous and Sandra E. Smith, describe as the calculated destruction of homes. Explaining the impetus for her piece, Salcedo pointed to current conflicts in Ukraine, Gaza, Syria, and Sudan, where people are being violently displaced en masse.

With House, Salcedo wanted to show that, while the dispossessed are of course vulnerable, they are also resilient. Her meshy nets are fragile and flexible, yet they are also much stronger than they seem. Hair may be ephemeral, but she makes it structural and sturdy. It’s all inspired, she told me, by the ways that spiders make webs of silk, material they take from their own bodies. Pairing hair and home, she evokes the ways that bodies and buildings—like dignity and domesticity—are tightly bound.

SALCEDO LEARNED TO WORK WITH human hair from earlier pieces: “Unland” (1995–98) comprises tables severed and then rearranged such that they depend on dissimilar tables for structural support. As if personifying the balancing act, the artist intricately threaded the surfaces with hair, drilling tiny holes in the tables to insert locks she gathered from a local salon. But for House, given its magnitude, she decided to source hair online, learning to look carefully for certain certificates, as there is a lot of violent crime in the human hair trade.

Hair is not the only tricky material that will feature in her fall show. On an upper floor of one of her studios, more assistants were at work on objects of a smaller scale, all destined for display alongside House at White Cube. They were wearing jeweler’s glasses and using X-Acto knives to meticulously remove the starch from individual grains of rice. A team of architects and engineers looked on, huddled around a computer on a lofted level as they worked out the structure of the sculpture’s shape. “I’ve never had such a large team,” she explained as I took in the scene. At one point, she tried working with a renowned engineer who eventually stepped down, saying the idea was too complicated.

When an artist uses sculpture’s most stalwart materials like wood or bronze—as Salcedo has in the past—“the tools are already designed for you,” she said. House required more trial and error than she’s ever needed before—so it also required her biggest team yet. “I had to fabricate new tools and new ways of working,” she explained as we watched assistants drill minuscule holes in starchless rice grains before passing them along to the next station, where still other assistants would thread individual hairs through those tiny openings. They were assembling a kind of mesh, then forming it around damaged cooking supplies—bowls and pots and pans—to form Grains of Sorrow (2023–26), a reminder of what is lost to domicide besides simple structure.

If this sounds like an incredibly elaborate—and surprisingly elegant—way to speak to tragedy, for Salcedo, both beauty and labor are part of her point. She is cognizant of how her studio might provide jobs to those who need them, employing, for instance, 150 women from the Colombian countryside, where it is difficult for them to find work.

The decision to both scale-up and work elaborately is as conceptual as it is material: “My work has always been labor-intensive because in the Global South, labor is intensive,” she said. “It’s completely different from industrialized countries.” She meant this not only as a way to shine a light on contemporary conditions, but also as a retort to art-historical tropes: Modernity is too often narrated, she said, as if “no single person from the Global South participated. But we know all the labor and all the suffering created modernity.” She wants to combine the forms and traditions of European sculpture with painstaking labor to show the two were always intertwined.

I asked her about the role beauty plays for her; she replied that she’s received a lot of criticism on this matter. She maintained, however, that “in all the violence and terror I’ve been researching all my life, I think the abject part belongs to the perpetrator,” adding that “beauty has a lot to do with dignity”—something she wants to restore as she tells the stories of victims. Elegance is also a way to get people to really look: The stories she’s telling are almost always in the newspapers, but that doesn’t mean everyone stops to soak them in. Salcedo doesn’t want you to divert your eyes from the world’s horrors, so she goes to extreme lengths to make sure you can’t look away.

#9041. 10 Signs You Might Not Really Be in Love: How to Tell the Difference

Love can feel like navigating a choose-your-own-adventure book with half the pages missing. Are you truly in love or just caught in a wave of infatuation? Sometimes, what seems like a heart-thumping romance may be a fleeting crush.

Wondering how to tell the difference? We’ve got you! Here’s a rundown of the 10 signs you’re not really in love.

Feeling a bit puzzled about your feelings for boo? That’s pretty normal. But before you start planning your future or picking out matching Halloween costumes, you may wanna make sure it’s real love and not a case of a serious crush.

Here are some signs that you may not really be in love:

Caught up in the romance novel vibe? If you’re all about the feelings of being in love rather than who’s sharing your popcorn, it might just be that you’re smitten with the idea of love itself.

Time to check if your relationship is more about the fairy tale than the real person.

Chatting with your partner shouldn’t feel as shallow as a kiddie pool. If deep talks are tougher than pulling teeth and rarer than a unicorn, it’s a red flag.

Sticking to small talk about the weather and dinner plans suggests the emotional depth for a lasting bond might be missing.

When discussions about future plans feel as far-fetched as sci-fi adventures, they may reveal underlying doubts about the relationship’s viability.

If imagining a future together feels unrealistic or undesirable, it’s time to ask yourself why. Real love plans a future; infatuation lives for the weekend.

Remember when their sock on the floor was cute? If little quirks now make you more cranky than charmed, it might mean the love goggles are off, your feelings have shifted from affection to annoyance, and the reality check has bounced.

Love is seeing imperfections and adoring them anyway.

Feeling more at ease or more ‘yourself’ when your partner isn’t around is a telling sign. If you’re secretly throwing mini-parties when they leave the room, you need to stop and think. Real-deal love means missing their chaos when they’re gone, not celebrating the silence.

Shared values are the anchor of deep, lasting relationships. If your core values clash more than a polka dot and stripes ensemble, you’re in for a rough ride, as finding common ground could be challenging!

Lasting love grows from shared beliefs and mutual respect, not from opposing battle lines.

No respect? No future. Respect is as critical to love as air is to breathing. Without mutual respect, you might just be coexisting rather than genuinely connecting.

If you no longer admire or respect each other’s opinions and choices, sustaining a healthy relationship will be difficult.

If they’re out of sight and totally out of mind, that’s not just independence — it might be indifference. When love is real, you should long for their laugh or lame jokes when they’re away. Could it be that your emotional attachment isn’t as strong as it should be for a lasting relationship?

If your best moments are consistently away from your partner, your heart might not be in it to win it. Perhaps your relationship isn’t providing enough support or happiness.

True love enriches your life and doesn’t play second fiddle to your social circle. It’s time to evaluate where your emotional energy is invested.

Still window shopping while you’re supposedly locked down? It’s a sign you might not be all in. A love that lasts doesn’t keep a backup catalog — it’s too busy loving what it already has.

Knowing why you’re still scanning for alternatives can help you address what might be missing or unfulfilled in your relationship.

Are you genuinely in love or just in love with being in love? If you’re secretly thrilled when they’re not around, stuck in surface-level chit-chat, or dreading deep-future talks, these are cosmic signs that it’s rethink o’clock.

Don’t ignore the signals — tuning in now can save you heartache later and lead you toward a love that genuinely fulfills you.

Last medically reviewed on June 26, 2024

#9040. Yinka Ilori reveals Tottenham Hotspur away shirt

Photography courtesy of Tottenham Hotspur Football Club

British-Nigerian designer Yinka Ilori has collaborated with Premier League football team Tottenham Hotspur to create a customised version of the club’s colourful away shirt.

Ilori reimagined the colourful away shirt, which was designed by Nike with a pattern of “never-before-seen visuals inspired by never-before-seen destinations”, by adding a graphic to the front and back.

On the front, in the position the sponsor logo is usually located, Ilori designed a circular motif combining the football club’s initials – THFC – with an abbreviation for London and the postcode for Tottenham, LDN17.

The lettering is bright orange with a white background.

On the rear of the shirt, Ilori created a graphic in his typical playful style around the letters COYS, which stands for Come On You Spurs.

Encircling the letters are the words “I know I am, I’m sure I am”, with the words “We are Tottenham wherever we go” around the whole graphic.

All of the lettering uses Ilori’s custom typeface, which was designed by type foundry British Standard Type for the designer in 2024.

According to the designer, who grew up in north London where the Populous-designed Tottenham Hotspur stadium is located, the collaboration aims to demonstrate the power of football to unite people.

“This project is a celebration of belonging and the power of football to bring people together,” said Ilori.

“For me, football is about the wider culture and the incredible sense of unity that comes from standing on the terraces, chanting alongside thousands of others,” he continued.

“I wanted the design to honour Tottenham Hotspur’s heritage while capturing that collective joy and spirit. The ‘Never Far From Home’ message really resonated with me, reflecting how football has the power to make you feel at home, wherever you are.”

The shirt is the latest design from the designer who has recently collaborated with brands including Brabantia and Veuve Clicquot.

Ilori also recently created a homeware and furniture collection for department store Dunelm.

Apartment D Films’ Cami Kwan discusses the intricate process behind the handcrafted film.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The fight for the Christmas advert crown is on, and brands have set standards high this year. From hand-drawn animation to immersive storytelling, there's been a wonderful display of hand-crafted creativity, and among the ranks, beauty brand e.l.f. did not disappoint.

As the brand's first-ever holiday campaign, the beautiful stop-motion animation is a sparkling debut that captures the joy of the festive season. A masterful display of tactile craftsmanship, the 'e.l.f. Made to Stand Out' campaign carries many of the traits of the best Christmas adverts, proving that analogue storytelling is the perfect tool for sparking festive joy.

Narrated by iconic actor Alan Cumming, the campaign follows friends Kit, Echo and Cleo as they reunite in their hometown for a holiday get-together. What could be an uncomfortable hangout turns into a celebration of the qualities that make them extraordinary, spreading festive cheer.

“For a campaign about the power of standing out, the medium needed to stand out too, and stop motion felt like such a natural fit for this story," explains Oshiya Savur, chief marketing officer at e.l.f. Beauty. "We're seeing a real appetite for nostalgia and a return to simpler times, with 72% of Americans saying nostalgic memories inspire them when life feels complicated.

There's an incredible level of craftsmanship and character that comes from building an entire world by hand

There's something about stop motion that takes you right back to the holiday specials you grew up watching, but we saw an opportunity to give that familiar art form a uniquely e.l.f. twist. There's an incredible level of craftsmanship and character that comes from building an entire world by hand, and when you combine that with our signature wit and wink, you create something that feels both familiar and completely unexpected.”

Created by Apartment D Films, each element of the ad reads as a love letter to analogue craft, from individually moulded characters to intricately constructed miniature sets. "We used a wide variety of different materials! It's truly a mixed media project," Cami Kwan, Creative Director of Apartment D, tells Creative Bloq. "The puppets have aluminium and steel wire armatures inside, which makes them posable. Their hands and heads are made of printed resin, which we then painted and finished with actual e.l.f. products! The cheeks and mouths of the puppets are colored using a combination of e.l.f. Powder Blush Palette, e.l.f Perfect 10 Eyeshadow Palette, and e.l.f. Halo Glow Silky Powder Highlighter.

All the characters' hair is made with different weights and textures of yarn, to call back to super nostalgic toys, but with a modern sensibility. The eyebrows and eyelids of the characters are made of a mix of wax and clay, so they're super mouldable to get big expressions in the performance, and also so you can literally see the animators' fingerprints on the characters as they emote.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

A lot of the world around the character is made of wood, but with hand-painted textures so the wood grain is more painterly and stylized. The mini products and bottles the characters use are all hand-sculpted out of clay, and then finished with a variety of nail art techniques, like cured acrylic, gels, and powder shimmers! The mini bottles are really so, so small; none of them is more than 1 inch tall."

It wasn't a project without some difficulties, as Cami explains. "One of our challenges was integrating real beauty products intended to live on human skin with stop-motion puppets. Unlike real humans, our puppets don't have pores and don't have a body temperature, both of which e.l.f. beauty products are chemically formulated to interact with.

On top of that, stop motion puppets are designed to be handled and touched constantly during the animation process, so the treatments and colors on them need to be incredibly resilient to constant wear and tear. We spent a good deal of time on the material testing of the e.l.f. beauty products to see which ones would integrate best with our fabrication techniques.

We're seeing a renewed appreciation for the analog, and I think that's a natural response to an increasingly digital world

It was actually really interesting to let our puppet team dip into their extensive knowledge of material science! We've found that generally anything based in a powder pigment merged really well with our typical techniques, and those combinations were really successful in getting puppets with a lot of character and a lot of dynamic color and shimmer on screen!"

Honouring such a tactile animation style is a time intensive practice, but are audiences hungry for analogue creativity? “Absolutely," says Oshiya. "The more purely AI-generated content we see, the greater the opposite and equal reaction from people craving something real: human connection and creativity they can actually feel.

We're seeing a renewed appreciation for the analogue, and I think that's a natural response to an increasingly digital world. At e.l.f., we're human first, human last. AI can be an incredible tool, but taste, discernment and original ideas come from human ingenuity. At the end of the day, we want to make people feel something, and that human element is what makes it possible.”

"The thing I'm most proud of is how kind and collaborative our crew on this project was. It's not something you can point to on screen, but it's something you can feel in how much care was taken with every frame, and how lively the animation is. There was so much joy in the creation and filming of this project, and I do think you can feel that in how kinetic and inventive everything is. It's a little zany, a little imperfect, and really so captivating when all seen together!" says Cami.

Every quirk and detail adds personality to the story, and there's no expectation of perfection.

"For a more specific on-screen detail, though, I love the smear frames we used when Echo is zooming between the tables and getting everyone amped up! Smear frames are an animation technique that's most typical in 2D animation – they're moments when, for just a few frames, you distort the character and literally smear them to give a sense of speed, mimicking the way something moving too fast on a live-action camera will appear blurry.

You hardly ever see smear frames in stop motion, but one of the things that we really focus on at Apartment D is pushing the stylistic boundaries of stop motion and finding ways to bring 2D animation techniques into our three-dimensional medium. So, in that Echo zooming scene, we actually used pieces of cut paper to create practical, dimensional smear frames! Jen Prokopowicz, the animator of that shot, curved the paper smears to get an extra sense of dimension, and created smears of different sizes to get a sense of speeding up and slowing down. It's just so cool, and something that generally only real animation nerds will notice," Kami adds.

“At e.l.f., we've never been interested in being part of a sea of sameness. We're a brand that celebrates the unexpected, embraces individuality and believes that what makes us different is what makes us extraordinary. That's what I love about stop motion. Every quirk and detail adds personality to the story, and there's no expectation of perfection. Just as no two handcrafted creations are exactly alike, no two people are either. It's a playful way to bring our belief in celebrating every eye, lip and face to life, and a reminder that your difference is low-key your gift,” says Oshiya.

#9038. Death Row’s Last Meals Anchor a Museum-Wide Survey of Incarceration Art

Louisiana State Penitentiary, known as “Angola” for the slave plantation that once occupied its land, lies at the dead end of Highway 66.

Past the gate, the road continues—invitation permitting—through 18,000 acres of penal farmland punctuated by gun towers, barbed-wire enclosures, and incarcerated men picking crops on the so-called farm line. America’s largest maximum-security prison, long notorious for its reliance on solitary confinement, Angola runs on the forgotten.

Gary Tyler, a fiber artist and activist, remembers Angola. He arrived in 1974 at seventeen years old, wrongly convicted of shooting a white student during a segregationist mob’s attack on his school bus. The prison is bound on three sides by bayou, bluffs, and swamp; escaping into one’s mind was easier. His grandmother was a quilter, he said, and fabric could be found or bartered. Time was given. Over four decades inside, including two stints on death row, he got good, even renowned. Craftswomen from across the South came to Angola to find the man behind the textiles making rounds outside. Related Articles Art en Route: Museum of London Eyes Trump Baby Balloon, Art Institute of Chicago Deaccessions Chinese Artworks, and More Other Voices, Other Worlds

“All that time, I never thought of myself as an ‘artist,’” Tyler said at the opening of “Rebirth,” a solo show of his quilted and appliquéd works at the Grand Rapids Art Museum. “I said, ‘Call me a hobbyist.’ Artists were people in galleries, people with an audience.”

“Rebirth” is one of three solo presentations on view in Grand Rapids through January 2027 that showcase art by or about people once incarcerated within the United States. Ray Materson, whose show is subtitled “Metamorphosis,” works in a medium he invented during his prison sentence for a drug-fueled robbery with a toy gun: palm-sized embroideries stitched by hand from the threads of unraveled socks, Americana meets Renaissance miniature.

The third show is The Last Supper, a 1,000-piece ceramic installation by the artist Julie Green, shown in its entirety for only the second time. For twenty years, up until their death in 2021, Green illustrated final-meal choices on ceramic plates painted in cobalt blue and re-fired in her kiln. What does the condemned order on death row? An overflowing bucket of Kentucky Fried Chicken, lobster, steak, burgers and fries, pecan pie. Nothing, sometimes: inmates can refuse or be denied a selection. (Final meal selections are generally a matter of public records.) At a quick glance, these plates might pass for Staffordshire. A closer look could ruin your lunch.

“It’s not so much that these shows are timely,” said Jennifer Wcisel, curator of collections at the Grand Rapids Art Museum. “It’s that the question of what incarceration means to American life is never absent. It’s ongoing.”

But has punishment been so openly advertised since the pre-Civil Rights era? Tennessee’s botched attempt to execute Christa Pike, the only woman on its death row, was followed by a magazine interview with the physician on hand to pronounce her dead (he said the state should try again). The Defense Secretary called for the military’s first execution in six decades—by firing squad—to be livestreamed. The White House launched an online arcade, where in one game a pixelated Border Patrol agent, rounds up “border crossers.”

The art can’t hope to match the volume of cruelty. It aspires to empathy or at least empathy’s catalyst: curiosity. Whose aim does a public execution serve? Within the carceral system, how is dignity doled out?

The Last Supper argues that dignity is a fickle allowance. Texas ended special last meals in 2011, after white supremacist Lawrence Russell Brewer ordered a feast and left it untouched. Set against Green’s terrible, tender plates, the result is hard to defend. Bite-size biographies like “he never had a birthday cake so we ordered a birth-day cake for him” give way to row upon row of “Standard prison fare.” This is dinnerware for a haunted house.

It is also a map of America’s patchwork principles on capital punishment. The Supreme Court barred executing people with intellectual disabilities in 2002, then left the states to define who qualifies, within limits. One plate records an IQ of 61, well below the benchmark of about 70, and a request that the menu not be released to the media. Another records a request that their meal be saved until after the execution.

Everything on view is portraiture, if the word can stretch to cover a spirit given a recognizable shape, even one abridged to a birthday cake. Tyler and Materson work with representational directness in the opposite register from Green. We see faces. Their work can indulge fantasy, the province of the living. One of Tyler’s quilts depicts a former inmate known as Big Toe in the so-called Greek Alps, still wearing the armor from The Life of Jesus Christ, a play produced by the drama club Tyler founded. Portraiture at its best is said to reveal the heart. For centuries it was also a privilege of the powerful, who commissioned likenesses to control how they were seen. Prison inverts that arrangement: the powerful do the watching. But what does surveillance ever capture of its subjects? Insight can’t be taken, only given.

Materson’s intricate embroideries stray in their subjects from baseball to outer space, with the most striking blending imagination and documentation. In Self-Portrait (undated), he sits before a mirror, stitching the very piece the viewer is looking at. Down a receding tunnel, a smaller Materson stitches a smaller Materson, and so on: infinity, or its likeness. The thick black frame that cages his face is made of the same thread as the rest, not impossibly undone.

One quilt late in Tyler’s show features a great crane, the kind that roosted in the wetlands around Angola and sometimes landed in the prison yard. Tyler was released in 2016, after decades of campaigning by activists including Rosa Parks. The crane captures that moment. His soul, he said, sprang skyward on his first step outside. It has yet to descend.

Tyler’s Convict Poker (2025) unfolds at the Angola prison rodeo: a Black man hangs in midair, bucked from a bull. The last of its kind in the country, the event is held twice a year and open to a paying public. Spectators can’t legally bet; the gamble belongs to the prisoners who volunteer. In convict poker, a raging bull is loosed on a mock card game, and the last man still seated wins a prize. Posting this October’s rodeo to Facebook, an attendee wrote: “The announcer said they didn’t run that fast from the PoPo 🚓😂 Watch til the end, prisoners were flying…”

Tyler never rode in the rodeo. But he doesn’t judge. (One of his quilts were raffled at the rodeo and raised $30,000 for the hospice program.) The men who volunteer, he said, are willing “to jeopardize their lives or go through a sense of degradation just to entertain an audience because nobody wants to be forgotten.”

“These are men who may never go home. The announcer mentions their names, and that they are serving life sentences; understand?”

#9037. Former workshop converted into contemporary Japanese home with "a sense of the passage of time"

Japanese studio Akio Isshiki Architects has transformed the home and workshop of a sheet-metal craftsperson in the castle town of Tatsuno into a modern house with a latticed wooden gate.

Architect Akio Isshiki, the founder of the eponymous studio, said he had to take a lot of different aspects into consideration when designing the project.

Among them was the location, as the two-storey home is located in a historic town known for being built around a medieval mountain castle.

“The project explores an architecture that responds naturally to the many contexts and conditions surrounding the house: the historic streetscape of the former castle town, traces of the former owner’s work as a sheet-metal craftsman, the client’s wishes, and practical constraints such as building regulations and structural requirements,” Isshiki told Dezeen.

For example, while the client had initially wanted a deck that would be connected to the dining room, the compact site made such a design difficult.

Instead, Isshiki removed part of the existing interior of the dining room to create a terrace space, which also includes a traditional-style engawa platform to connect the home with the garden.

Here, the studio added a sliding glass door that was designed so that its frame is hidden in the wall when it is closed, creating the impression of a fully open space.

Isshiki also wanted the 144-square-metre contemporary home to nod to more traditional Japanese houses.

“To sit comfortably within the townscape that retains the character of a former castle town, the spatial principles of traditional machiya – Japanese old townhouses – have been incorporated into this contemporary residence,” he explained.

“Examples include a long approach leading towards a bright garden at the back of the house, and an engawa, a narrow platform that connects the interior with the garden.”

The former workshop in front of the house was treated as a public-facing space. Where it looks onto the street, Isshiki added a large latticed, sliding gate, made from cedar, as well as a narrow entrance porch.

Inside, this multi-functional space becomes almost like an enclosed terrace. Here, Isshiki also added a small wooden toilet, inspired by those found in traditional machiya houses.

The studio kept a number of objects that were found in the old workshop, including a metal ring that now decorates a handrail next to the indoor staircase.

Isshiki relocated this staircase so that it sits at the front of the house, in the old workshop space – one of the biggest changes made to the layout of the house. A stone underneath the first step provides a space to remove footwear.

Isshiki’s studio used wood throughout the renovation, as the original building was made from timber and this material worked best with the existing neighbourhood, including a historic shrine that stands directly across from the house.

“The newly added wood, including the doors, is cedar, which is also the primary wood used in the original structure,” Isshiki said.

“Cedar is one of the most widely used types of wood in Japan and is readily available,” he continued.

“The contrast between the lighter new cedar and the existing cedar, which has darkened with age, brings a sense of the passage of time to the house.”

Akio Isshiki Architects also used earthen plasterwork in the home to create a tactile feel, while Tunisian tiles add decorative patterns in the kitchen. Here, the studio also created a built-in, combined wooden dining table and work surface.

On the top floor, which has a bedroom, living room and guest room, the studio mostly kept the original layout.

However, it added a sunken study space and a tokonoma, a recessed area used to display flowers and pieces of art.

“Through careful consideration of spatial dimensions, light, connections to the outdoors, materials, details, and relationships between spaces, the aim was to create a home that feels comfortable as a whole,” Isshiki concluded about the renovation.

His studio has previously designed a charred-cedar-clad house in Osaka and married old and new within a combined home and restaurant.

#9036. Say What? 7 Tips to Unclog Your Blocked Ears

Earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure might be behind your clogged ears. There are many easy ways to get relief at home.

Whether it’s from a cold, allergies, or changes in air pressure, blocked ears can disrupt your day-to-day activities and even cause discomfort. Thankfully, there are several effective methods to help unclog your ears and restore your hearing. Listen up!

Why are my ears clogged?

Clogging can happen either on the inside or the outside of your eardrum. Here are the most common ways your ears can get blocked:

  • Earwax in the outer ear helps prevent particles and excess water from entering the middle ear. However, if earwax builds up too much outside the eardrum, it can cause a blockage.
  • If you’ve been swimming recently, some water might be stuck in your ear canal, pushing against your eardrum. When that water hangs around too long, it can lead to a swimmer’s ear, an outer ear infection.
  • Sinus infections, ear infections, and Eustachian tube dysfunction can pressure your eardrum’s inner side.
  • Allergies can cause uncomfortable inflammation and congestion in your ears. Your sinuses, throat, and ears are connected, so when you feel stuffed up and sniffly, your inner ear feels the pain too.
  • Changes in air pressure, like when you fly, can cause uncomfortable ear pressure.

Best clogged ear remedies

1. Pop and unclog

The easiest way to unclog your ears is by “popping” them. Just pinch your nose shut, seal your lips, and gently blow. This simple technique, known as the Valsalva maneuver, won’t clear earwax or fluid but is a common trick people use on planes.

2. Swallow, yawn, or chew

The Eustachian tubes connect your middle ear to the back of your throat. They briefly open when you swallow, yawn, or chew. Altitude changes can cause these tubes to close, but chewing gum or yawning can help reopen them. Alternatively, you can try the Toynbee maneuver, where you hold your nose and swallow.

3. Ear drops

Over-the-counter (OTC) ear drops can soften and dissolve excess earwax. If you prefer a DIY approach, warm a small amount of mineral oil and use an eye dropper to apply a few drops into your ear for a few minutes.

Pro tip: Baby oil or olive oil can also be used, but make sure it’s not too hot. Additionally, diluted hydrogen peroxide drops can be helpful.

4. Warmth and gravity

To loosen up clogged earwax, use a warm, damp washcloth as a compress. Lie down with the clogged ear facing down against the heated washcloth. Gravity and heat will help the earwax move along more easily.

5. Hit the steam room

Steam can help drain sinuses and alleviate pressure in your inner ear. Close the bathroom door, let the hot shower run for a while, and then luxuriate with deep, cleansing breaths. 

6. Take allergy medication

Because your throat, sinuses, and ears are interconnected, any sickness affecting your sinuses or throat can also impact your ears.

Over-the-counter antihistamines, decongestants, or nasal sprays can relieve sniffles, coughs, and ear discomfort.

7. Rinse away the gunk

Rinsing your nasal passages with a medication-free saline solution can help reduce congestion and clear out mucus that might be causing ear blockage. You can also consider investing in a nasal irrigation system for more thorough mucus clearing.

When to see your doctor

Have you been unable to unclog your ears for a few days, or are you experiencing severe pain, fever, dizziness, hearing loss, fluid discharge, or unusual odor? If so, it’s crucial to contact your healthcare provider promptly. These symptoms may indicate an infection that needs medical attention.

What not to do when you have clogged ears

  • Cotton swabs: Q-tips and other cotton swabs to remove earwax can push it further into your ear canal, so don’t do it. 
  • Candling: Ear candles might seem like a fun party trick, but there’s no science to prove they work, and they’ve been shown to cause injuries.
  • Sprays: Decongestant nasal sprays can be helpful, but using them too long can lead to rebound congestion.
  • Drying solutions: A few drops of rubbing alcohol or a mixture of one part vinegar and one part alcohol can help dry out the ears when you have a swimmer’s ear. However, doing this regularly can lead to irritation.

Takeaway

Clogged ears are often caused by earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure. You can use over-the-counter or DIY ear drops, irrigation kits, or warm compresses to unblock your ears. Antihistamines or nasal sprays can also help relieve clogs caused by allergies.

PSA: Consult a healthcare provider if your blocked ears are painful or at-home remedies don’t work.

Cathay Pacific or Qantas Business Class via Alaska Mileage Plan — no fuel surcharges

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Picture this: you're reclining in a fully flat bed at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Pacific, a glass of Château Léoville Barton in hand, watching the Australian coastline slowly materialize through your window. The cabin is hushed. The seat — Cathay Pacific's renowned Business Class throne on the Airbus A350-1000 — cocoons you in a private pod with a sliding door, direct aisle access, and a mattress pad that makes a five-star hotel bed feel like an afterthought. This is the LAX–HKG–SYD route in Cathay Pacific Business Class. And you booked it for 55,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles. Now consider what the person three rows up in economy paid in cash for their seat — and what the couple beside you in business paid for theirs. A Cathay Pacific Business Class ticket on this route typically retails between **$5,000 and $12,000**. That's not a typo. Premium cabin pricing on transpacific routes is notoriously aggressive, and Australia amplifies it further because of the sheer distance involved. At 55,000 miles for a one-way business class redemption, you're extracting somewhere between **9.1 and 21.8 cents per point (CPP)** — a range that makes most loyalty program strategists stop and stare. The ChooseFI community benchmarks a "good" redemption at 1.5–2 CPP for most programs. You are obliterating that benchmark. At the high end of this range, 55,000 miles is doing the work of $12,000 in cash. That is what the FI mindset calls asymmetric value. This is also a premium *experience*, not just a premium number. Cathay Pacific consistently ranks among the world's top airlines for business class. The A350-1000 is their flagship long-haul aircraft, featuring a 1-2-1 configuration with every single seat having direct aisle access. There are no middle seats. There are no awkward climbs over sleeping strangers. There is a full dine-on-demand menu, a curated wine list, noise-canceling headphones, and a ground service team that treats you like a valued guest before you even board. For the FI traveler, this redemption represents something rare: a genuine luxury experience — the kind that recalibrates your sense of what travel can feel like — made nearly free through a well-understood system. The math works. The experience delivers. And once you've done it, you'll understand exactly why the ChooseFI community talks about this one.

Alaska Mileage Plan is one of the most valuable frequent flyer programs in the world despite being a relatively small airline. The secret is their partner award chart: Alaska uses fixed pricing for partner airline awards, meaning costs do not fluctuate with demand the way dynamic programs do. This creates structural pricing inefficiencies — especially on premium cabin routes to Asia and Oceania — that savvy travelers can exploit. Alaska has partnerships with Cathay Pacific, Qantas, Japan Airlines, Emirates, Fiji Airways, and others. The primary way to earn Alaska miles is through the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature card (Bank of America), through flying, or via Marriott Bonvoy transfers at a 3:1 ratio.

Free calculator shows when you could reach financial independence — plus a savings rate tracker, expense audit, and more.

Here's the insight that transforms this from "interesting" to "actionable": Alaska Airlines Mileage Plan uses a fixed partner award chart, and that chart prices Cathay Pacific Business Class to Australia at 55,000 miles one-way — a number that hasn't kept pace with the explosive cash price inflation of premium cabin fares.

Most major U.S. loyalty programs have migrated to dynamic pricing, where award costs fluctuate with cash fare demand. Alaska hasn't done this for partner awards. Their chart is fixed. That means when Cathay Pacific's cash fares spike to $12,000 during Australian school holidays or peak summer travel, your award cost stays exactly where it was: 55,000 miles. This is the pricing inefficiency at the heart of this redemption, and it's why the ChooseFI community treats Alaska Mileage Plan as one of the most valuable programs in the industry.

Alaska Mileage Plan has only one meaningful transfer partner for most people: Marriott Bonvoy, at a ratio of 3 Bonvoy points to 1 Alaska mile. That's a steep ratio — you'll need 165,000 Bonvoy points to generate 55,000 Alaska miles — and transfer times run 1 to 5 days, so plan accordingly. There is no direct credit card transfer path into Alaska Mileage Plan from Chase, Amex, or Citi, which is why the "Easy to Earn" score for this redemption is a 2 out of 5. The miles must be earned directly: through Alaska's co-branded credit card (the Alaska Airlines Visa from Bank of America), through flying Alaska or its partners, or via Marriott transfer.

This is crucial and often overlooked. Alaska charges no fuel surcharges on any partner award bookings. This matters enormously for a Cathay Pacific redemption. If you were to book the same Cathay flight through Cathay's own Asia Miles program or through British Airways Avios, you could face fuel surcharges of $400–$900 or more on top of the points cost. With Alaska, your out-of-pocket cost is taxes and fees only — typically in the range of $50–$150 depending on the routing. That's it. A $12,000 experience for 55,000 miles and roughly $100 in fees.

Alaska allows a free stopover on one-way awards — a benefit that is genuinely rare among U.S. programs. On the LAX–HKG–SYD routing, this means you can build a stopover in Hong Kong at no additional points cost. Spend a few days exploring one of the world's most dynamic cities — the markets of Mong Kok, the skyline from Victoria Peak, the dim sum temples of Kowloon — then board your continuing flight to Sydney. Two destinations. One redemption. Same 55,000 miles.

The 55,000-mile rate applies to both Cathay Pacific and Qantas for business class to Australia. Cathay routes you through Hong Kong (HKG); Qantas has its own metal and routing options. If Cathay availability is thin, checking Qantas can open up alternatives without changing your points cost.

Do not start at Alaska's website. Alaska's own search tool for partner availability can be unreliable for Cathay Pacific. Instead, go to ba.com (British Airways' booking site) and run a one-way business class search for your desired route — for example, LAX to SYD or LAX to HKG. British Airways and Cathay Pacific are oneworld partners, and BA's search engine surfaces Cathay award availability with remarkable accuracy. Look for "Reward" seats in the business class (Club World or equivalent) cabin. Any dates showing availability on BA.com are almost certainly bookable through Alaska as well. Screenshot or note the specific dates before moving on.

Alaska opens its award booking window 331 days in advance. If you're targeting peak travel dates — Australian summer (December–February), for example — set a calendar reminder to search and transfer 331 days ahead. Your miles also never expire in Mileage Plan, which gives you flexibility to accumulate without pressure.

Confirm you have at least 55,000 Alaska miles available. If you're converting Marriott Bonvoy points, you'll need 165,000 Bonvoy points at the 3:1 ratio. Initiate transfers at least one week before you plan to call, as Marriott-to-Alaska transfers can take 1 to 5 days.

Log into your Marriott Bonvoy account, navigate to "Transfer Points," select Alaska Airlines as the recipient program, and enter your Mileage Plan number. Transfer in increments of 3,000 Bonvoy points (yielding 1,000 Alaska miles). Do not transfer until you've confirmed availability in Step 1 — points transfers are generally non-reversible.

This redemption cannot be booked online — Alaska's web portal does not support all partner award bookings, particularly for Cathay Pacific. Call Alaska Airlines at 1-800-252-7522. Tell the agent:

Have your Mileage Plan number, passport information, and a credit card for the taxes and fees ready. The call typically takes 20–40 minutes. Agents are generally knowledgeable, but if you encounter confusion, politely ask for a senior agent or call back.

If Cathay availability is limited on your preferred dates, ask the agent to check Qantas availability to Australia at the same 55,000-mile rate. Qantas Business (The Business) has its own award inventory and may have open seats when Cathay is fully allocated.

If you're routing through Hong Kong on Cathay, explicitly ask the agent to add a free stopover at HKG. This is a program benefit, not a favor — Alaska's routing rules allow one free stopover on one-way awards. Specify how many nights you want in Hong Kong before the continuing flight to Sydney.

The best way to find Cathay Pacific Business Class award availability is through the British Airways website (ba.com). Search for one-way flights from your U.S. gateway to Sydney or Melbourne, and look for dates showing Cathay Pacific-operated flights with Business Class availability. British Airways shows oneworld partner availability more reliably than most tools.

If Cathay Pacific shows no availability on your preferred dates, search for Qantas Business Class on the same route. Qantas availability can be found through the Qantas website or through British Airways. The Alaska Mileage Plan price is the same 55,000 miles for either carrier.

Earn miles through the Alaska Airlines Visa card sign-up bonus (typically 60,000 to 75,000 miles), through flying Alaska or partners, or by transferring from Marriott Bonvoy. If transferring from Marriott, allow 1 to 5 business days for the transfer to complete before your booking window closes.

Call Alaska Mileage Plan at 1-800-252-7522 and request a partner award booking on Cathay Pacific (or Qantas) Business Class. Provide your desired dates and routing. Ask about adding a free stopover in Hong Kong if routing through HKG. The agent will process the booking and deduct 55,000 miles plus taxes and fees (typically $50 to $150).

After booking through Alaska, manage your seat selection directly through the Cathay Pacific website or app using your booking reference. Select a window or aisle seat in the 1-2-1 configuration — every seat has direct aisle access, so there is no wrong choice. You can also pre-order meals and manage other preferences through Cathay's platform.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Let's make this concrete. You and your partner want to celebrate a milestone — a sabbatical, a paid-off mortgage, financial independence itself — with a trip to Sydney. Here's exactly how this redemption plays out.

The Route: Los Angeles (LAX) → Hong Kong (HKG) → Sydney (SYD), on Cathay Pacific Business Class, with a 3-night stopover in Hong Kong.

Cash Price: A quick search on Google Flights confirms what you suspected — this itinerary in business class retails for approximately $8,000 per person during the shoulder season. During the Australian summer or holiday periods, it climbs closer to $11,000–$12,000.

Your Cost: 55,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles + approximately $85 in taxes and fees. Per person.

CPP Calculation: At $8,000 cash value, your 55,000 miles are worth 14.5 cents per point — more than seven times what you'd get redeeming Alaska miles for domestic economy. At $12,000, you're at 21.8 cents per point, which is among the highest CPP figures available anywhere in the U.S. loyalty ecosystem.

In Hong Kong, Cathay Pacific's The Pier Business Class Lounge awaits during your stopover travel. It's widely regarded as one of the finest airport lounges in the world — noodle bar, live cooking stations, a spa treatment center, and a wine selection that rivals dedicated restaurants.

After three days exploring Hong Kong, you reboard for the six-hour SYD leg, arriving in Sydney ready — genuinely ready, not depleted — to start your adventure.

Total cost for two: 110,000 Alaska miles + roughly $170 in fees. That's the FI mindset applied to travel: extraordinary experiences made nearly free through a system anyone can learn.

Alaska's booking window opens 331 days out. Cathay Pacific releases business class award space to partner programs in limited quantities, and the best dates disappear quickly. Set a calendar alert for 331 days before your target travel date and be ready to search — and call — that morning.

The single best technique for this redemption: run your search on ba.com before calling Alaska. BA's search engine is faster, more reliable for Cathay availability, and lets you visually scan a full month of dates. Identify two or three date options before you pick up the phone. This dramatically shortens your call time and reduces the chance of getting an agent who says "I'm not seeing anything."

Don't treat the Hong Kong stopover as a layover — treat it as a destination. Alaska's routing rules explicitly allow a free stopover on one-way awards. Two to four nights in Hong Kong costs you nothing extra in miles. Pair this with a cheap positioning flight or use it as an anchor for a broader Asia itinerary.

This is the most common and most painful mistake. Marriott-to-Alaska transfers are generally not reversible. If you transfer 165,000 Bonvoy points to Alaska and then discover no award space exists on your dates, you're stuck with miles you may not use optimally. Always confirm availability on ba.com before initiating any transfer.

Book two one-way redemptions rather than a round-trip. This gives you full flexibility on return routing — you might come back on Qantas through another city, or extend your trip without penalty.

Since there are no major flexible currency transfer paths into Alaska (no Chase, Amex, or Citi transfers), the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature from Bank of America is your most efficient earning vehicle. The welcome bonus alone can cover a significant portion of this redemption. Pair with everyday spending in categories that earn elevated miles.

If Cathay availability is closed on your dates, Qantas Business Class to Australia prices at the same 55,000 miles. Qantas' "The Business" product on their A380 Sydney routes is exceptional in its own right — and availability patterns differ from Cathay, so checking both genuinely doubles your options.

This redemption is purpose-built for the FI-minded couple or solo traveler who is willing to invest some effort in the booking process in exchange for an extraordinary, nearly free experience. If you've been dreaming about Australia and refuse to pay $8,000–$12,000 for a business class ticket — but you're also not willing to spend 20+ hours crammed in economy for a trip this significant — this is your answer.

Minimum requirements: You need 55,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles per person. For two travelers, that's 110,000 miles. If you're building from zero through the Alaska Visa, factor in 6–12 months of earning runway before booking.

Within a broader FI travel strategy, this redemption pairs well with a Marriott Bonvoy credit card for point accumulation and an Alaska Visa for direct mile earning. It's a medium-complexity move with a very high ceiling on value.

This redemption earns a **moderate difficulty rating** — and that rating is honest. It's not complicated in concept, but it has two specific friction points that trip up even experienced travel rewards enthusiasts. **Challenge 1: Earning the Miles** Alaska Mileage Plan's isolation from major flexible currency programs (no Chase Ultimate Rewards, no Amex Membership Rewards, no Citi ThankYou transfers directly) means you can't simply funnel points you already have into Alaska. The primary path is the Alaska Airlines Visa (Bank of America) or a Marriott Bonvoy conversion at an unfavorable 3:1 ratio. Plan your earning strategy well in advance. **Tip:** Prioritize the Alaska Visa signup bonus as your foundation, then supplement with Marriott points if needed. **Challenge 2: The Phone Booking Requirement** You cannot book this online. The call-in process intimidates people who've only ever booked travel digitally. **Tip:** Do your homework on ba.com first, have your dates ready, and approach the call as an informed customer — not someone asking for help finding availability. Agents respond well to specific, prepared callers. **Challenge 3: Cathay Award Availability** Cathay Pacific releases partner award space selectively and often in small quantities. Availability rated 3/5. **Tip:** Search exactly at the 331-day booking window, keep Qantas as your backup at the same price point, and be flexible with travel dates by even one or two days — a Tuesday departure often has inventory when Saturday doesn't. The good news: once you've done this once, you'll understand the system deeply enough to replicate it. The ChooseFI community has members who've booked this exact route multiple times. The first time takes effort. After that, it's a process you know cold.

The fastest path is the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature card from Bank of America, which typically offers a 60,000 to 75,000-mile sign-up bonus. That alone nearly covers the 55,000 miles needed. You can also transfer Marriott Bonvoy points at 3:1 (165,000 Bonvoy points equals 55,000 Alaska miles) or earn miles through flying Alaska and its partners.

Yes. You would book two separate one-way awards at 55,000 miles each. You could fly Cathay Pacific one direction and Qantas the other, or mix carriers based on availability. Each one-way can include its own free stopover.

Cathay Pacific typically releases Business Class award space 90 to 330 days before departure. The sweet spot for finding availability is usually 90 to 120 days out, when airlines release unsold premium cabin seats. Check frequently, as availability can appear and disappear quickly.

Alaska allows one free stopover on one-way awards. On a routing from the US to Australia via Hong Kong, you can stop in Hong Kong for any number of days at no additional miles cost. Simply tell the agent when booking that you want a stopover in HKG. This effectively gives you two destinations for the price of one redemption.

The Alaska Mileage Plan redemption for Cathay Pacific or Qantas Business Class to Australia is one of the most extraordinary sweet spots in travel rewards. At 55,000 miles for a seat that costs $5,000 to $12,000 in cash — with zero fuel surcharges and a free stopover in Hong Kong — this redemption delivers 9 to 22 cents per point. It requires more planning and effort than a simple hotel booking, but the payoff is a genuine luxury travel experience that proves the asymmetric value the FI community builds its travel rewards strategy around.

#9033. Are Tangerines Good for You? 5 Health Benefits You Might Love

Tangerines are not just tasty — they’re a powerhouse of nutrients. Packed with tangy flavor and vibrant orange color, these citrus delights offer a host of health benefits. From boosting your immune system to rejuvenating your skin, tangerines are nutrient-rich allies for your well-being. Let’s delve into their nutritional profile and discover why they’re a smart addition to your diet.

Tangerines are nutritional powerhouses. Here’s what each of these little champs pack under their orange belts:

Tangerines are teeny cousins of the orange but with a thinner, easier-to-peel skin. They boast a sweet and juicy flavor and pack a ton of vitamins, particularly vitamin C, as well as minerals like potassium, antioxidants, and dietary fiber.

These tiny bursts of sunshine have many benefits that can significantly enhance your health. Here’s why you might want to make tangerines a regular part of your diet:

Tangerines are loaded with vitamin C, turning them into tiny, tasty guardians for your health. This crucial vitamin supercharges your immune system by enhancing the function and effectiveness of white blood cells, which are essential for fighting off pathogens and infections. By improving the activity and response of these cells, vitamin C helps your body combat a wide range of infections more effectively.

Therefore, regular consumption of these mini-oranges satisfies your taste buds and boosts your body’s defense mechanisms — a win-win!

Want that glow? Tangerines have got you covered. They’re high in potassium, a real game-changer for regulating hydration and balancing fluid levels in your skin cells. This essential mineral keeps your skin cells plump and hydrated, warding off pesky, dry, dull patches.

Plus, potassium supports the removal of toxins and wastes, which means clearer, more radiant skin.

Tangerines are also a fantastic source of vitamin A, which strengthens the outer layer of your skin, smoothing out wrinkles and reducing fine lines. Along with vitamin C, it’s a potent antioxidant, protecting your skin from the damaging and aging effects of free radicals.

Are you having tummy troubles? Tangerines can help with a fiber boost that keeps things moving smoothly along your digestive tract.

These zesty little superheroes are your gut’s new best friends. They’re loaded with fiber that bulks up and softens things down there, making your bathroom visits smooth and speedy. This fruity fix helps manage everything from irregular pit stops to those bloated bleurgh days.

Fiber also balances your gut flora, promoting a healthy microbial environment in your intestines. This balance is crucial for optimal digestion, nutrient absorption, and immune function.

So, grab a tangerine to remedy your belly blues next time your gut feels out of whack.

Tangerines are a dynamo when it comes to battling serious health baddies like cancer and heart disease. These little orange wonders are loaded with flavonoids, natural compounds that help with heart health and cancer prevention.

Flavonoids help relax the blood vessels, lowering blood pressure levels and reducing the strain on your heart. This helps keep your ticker ticking smoothly and reduces the risk of cardiovascular diseases like heart attacks and strokes.

But wait, there’s more! When it comes to cancer, flavonoids mess with the bad guys — cancer cells — stopping them from multiplying and spreading their nonsense around your body.

Keep your peepers sharp with a dose of vitamin A from tangerines. This essential nutrient and compounds like beta-carotene shield your eyes from age-related issues and support healthy vision. It plays a key role in creating rhodopsin, a protein in your eyes that allows you to see in low-light conditions.

Munching on tangerines helps keep your night vision in superhero shape and supports overall eye function, keeping your peepers sharp and responsive.

Furthermore, tangerines contain other essential eye health nutrients, like lutein and zeaxanthin. These antioxidants are found in high concentrations in the retina, where they help filter blue light and prevent oxidative damage, further protecting the eyes from conditions like cataracts.

Sure, tangerines are delish and make your taste buds do a happy dance, but they’re also packed with nutrients that can seriously amp up your well-being.

From giving your immune system a high-five to keeping your heart beating like a healthy drum, tangerines are basically wellness wrapped in a bright orange peel. So, go grab one and make it your main squeeze!

Last medically reviewed on June 26, 2024

#9032. Holst completes Adjaye-designed mass-timber library in Oregon

Photography by Christian Columbres

US architecture studio Holst has created a mass-timber library in Oregon, with a series of tall columns at the entrance and a central atrium, after taking over the project from Adjaye Associates.

The East County Library in Gresham features a trapezoidal roof structure on top of a mostly square building envelope, creating multi-storey covered entry programmes on each side.

These entry programmes are lined with massive glued-laminated (glulam) mass-timber columns that Holst said speak to a primary effect of the design: “awe and accessibility”.

“One of our major main vision points of the project was this idea of awe and accessibility,” Holst principal and creative director Brittany Shreiner told Dezeen.

Shreiner said that the accessible component comes from the dual entry programmes that open up to a plaza on one side, with space taken from a converted street, and an elevated entryway on the other that features ramps.

A rail line is located on one side and a bus line on the other, connecting the building to the wider public realm.

For the team, the building needed to be a “big civic moment”, thus the massive columned entryway. However, Shreiner said that the awe the studio aspired to create was more akin to that of a forest, and the mass timber helped them to express that.

Structurally, the building has a mix of concrete and mass timber elements, with mostly wooden floorplates and some walls, and concrete-and-steel cores.

The facade is a mix of vertical timber elements interspaced with high-performance concrete bands with scalloped shapes and vertical bands of glass.

At one point, a grey-toned concrete panelling system marks the semi-circular protrusion where the structure’s amphitheatre is.

The appearance of the building is close to the original design submitted by Adjaye Associates – Holst was the architect of record at the start.

However, after misconduct allegations against Adjaye Associates founder David Adjaye were made public in a Financial Times investigation, the studio was released from this project, among others. Adjaye denies the allegations.

Shriener said that the biggest changes in the design were the removal of screens that were supposed to overhang from the covered entryways and a tower that extended past the roof plane.

“There was still a lot of design to be done [at that time], but the bones of the building were there. The community buy-in was there. The stakeholder buy-in was there,” said Shriener.

“So, the county was definitely clear in their intention that they did not want to proceed with Adjaye as part of our team, and that they basically trusted us to bring the project forward, but they didn’t want to see a total redesign by any means.”

Having recently solidified itself as a name in the US mass timber game with a tall building in Portland, the studio focused on optimising the timber usage as it took over the design. It worked closely with local mass-timber supplier TimberLab for the materials.

One detail that stands out is the notches in the timber columns and beams that give the structure a cabin-like or residential appearance, while remaining monumental in scale.

More than just a style conceit, the notches play a role in the ceiling plane, hiding the mechanical systems and lighting.

Inside, vestibules compress the entry to the library, which then opens up into a main core that runs between the entrances, with a double-height atrium space in the middle, complete with a wood-slatted spiral staircase.

For Shriener, this middle space represents a “clearing” in the forest.

The primary book-storage spaces surround the main central area, with smaller breakout rooms and classrooms lying mostly on the perimeter.

Mass-timber elements remain visible throughout the interior spaces, with green carpets at times continuing the forest metaphor.

On the roof, a series of sawtooth lightwells bring diffuse light into the main central space, while a rooftop patio allows guests to enjoy the views of the mountains beyond.

Elsewhere in Oregon, Holst created a Gaudí-informed apartment building wrapped in wood.

Other projects that were completed after the fallout from the Adjaye allegations include the Princeton Art Museum, where David Adjaye “stepped back” from the project in the late stages, according to Princeton.
